poets.name: Cynewulf
poets.credit: The runic signature of Cynewulf woven into the text of his poem ‘The Fates of the Apostles,’ Vercelli Book, folio 54r, 10th century — not a portrait (none survives), but the poet's own cryptographic signature in runes, the only trace of his identity. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Cynewulf is one of only a handful of Old English poets known to us by name — not from any external record, but because he wove his own name in runic letters into the closing lines of four poems, as a kind of signed prayer for the reader's intercession.

Nothing certain is known of his life, not even his precise dates; scholars place him anywhere from the 8th to the 9th century based on his language and dialect. The four poems bearing his runic signature are Juliana and Christ II (the Ascension) in the Exeter Book, and Elene and The Fates of the Apostles in the Vercelli Book — all religious verse composed in the traditional alliterative meter inherited from pre-Christian heroic poetry.

Generations of scholars once attributed much more of the Old English corpus to him — Andreas, the Guthlac poems, The Phoenix, The Dream of the Rood — on stylistic grounds, but only the four signed poems can be assigned to him with confidence.

poets.name: Cædmon
poets.credit: A page from the so-called ‘Cædmon Manuscript’ (Bodleian Library, MS Junius 11, c. 1000) — the illustrated Old English paraphrase of Genesis, Exodus, and Daniel once (wrongly) believed to be Cædmon's own work. Not a portrait; no image of him survives. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Cædmon is the first English poet known to us by name. According to the Venerable Bede's Ecclesiastical History (completed 731), he was an illiterate herdsman attached to the double monastery at Whitby who, ashamed of his inability to sing at feasts, received the gift of song in a dream: a stranger commanded him to “sing of the beginning of created things,” and he woke with the verses of what is now called Cædmon's Hymn already composed.

The Abbess Hild, recognizing the gift as divine, had him instructed in sacred history so that he might turn it into verse; he is said to have gone on to compose poems on Genesis, Exodus, and other scriptural subjects, though none of these survive under his name. Only the nine-line Hymn, preserved by Bede and copied into manuscripts of the Ecclesiastical History, can be attributed to him with any confidence.

For centuries the long biblical paraphrases of the Junius Manuscript (Genesis, Exodus, Daniel, Christ and Satan) were attributed to Cædmon on the strength of Bede's account, and the manuscript is still nicknamed for him, but modern scholarship treats those poems as the anonymous work of later, unrelated poets.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old English)
poets.credit: A full page of the Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library, MS 3501, c. 970–990) carrying the poem ‘Deor’ — one of the four great codices in which nearly the whole surviving corpus of Old English poetry is preserved. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The great majority of surviving Old English poetry is anonymous. It comes down to us almost entirely through four manuscripts copied around the late 10th and early 11th centuries — the Exeter Book, the Vercelli Book, the Junius Manuscript, and the Nowell Codex (which also contains Beowulf) — plus a few poems preserved elsewhere, such as in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

These poets, working in the alliterative, four-stress long line inherited from a common Germanic tradition, left behind elegies of exile and loss (The Wanderer, The Seafarer, The Wife's Lament), heroic fragments (The Battle of Maldon, The Fight at Finnsburg), riddles, saints' lives, and biblical paraphrase, alongside the single most revered poem of the corpus, The Dream of the Rood.

This entry gathers the many unsigned Old English poems in this archive — as distinct from Beowulf's anonymous poet, Cædmon, and the runically-signed Cynewulf — under one umbrella, in keeping with how they survive: unattributed, and copied by scribes who did not think to record whose voice they were preserving.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old Irish)
poets.credit: Folio 53 of the Book of Leinster (c. 1160) · No portrait exists for anonymous poets; a manuscript page is shown instead · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The early Irish poems gathered here were composed in Old and Middle Irish between roughly the eighth and the twelfth centuries, mostly by unnamed monks, scribes, hermits and court poets. They survive in medieval manuscripts such as the Book of Leinster and Lebor na hUidre, and many are tied by tradition to figures such as St Patrick, Colum Cille, Moling or King Cormac, though those attributions are legendary and the poems are treated here as anonymous.

The selection runs from sagas and the otherworld voyage of Bran to hymns, hermit songs, nature lyrics, love poems, bardic laments and the quatrains scribes wrote in the margins of their books, among them the poem of the monk and his cat Pangur. The English versions are by the Celtic scholar Kuno Meyer, from Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (London, 1911).

poets.name: Classical Japanese Poets
poets.credit: Kakinomoto no Hitomaro, from the Sanjūrokkasen-gaku (Thirty-six Immortal Poets) by Kanō Tan'yū, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). An imagined likeness; no contemporary portrait of any of these poets survives.
bio: The poems collected here are the earliest voices of Japanese verse in this archive: ballads, love songs, elegies and short stanzas of the seventh to tenth centuries, the Nara and early Heian courts. Some carry the names of court poets, among them Hitomaro, Akahito, Okura, Sosei, Narihira and the Lady Komachi; many are anonymous, and a few are given only to a title or an editorial line. Because most of the named poets have just one to three pieces apiece, the archive gathers them under a single entry, and each poem's note gives its author exactly as the source prints it.

All the poems are in English by Basil Hall Chamberlain, taken from the 'Classical Poetry of Japan' section of the anthology Japanese Literature (The Colonial Press, 1900). Chamberlain turns the Japanese into rhymed English verse, so the five-and-seven-syllable counts of the originals are not kept; the Japanese long poems become ballad stanzas and the short poems become four-line stanzas. Dates here are approximate, as the volume gives none for its poets.

poets.name: Po Chü-i
poets.credit: Portrait of Bai Juyi (白樂天), traditional Chinese painting · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Po Chü-i (Bai Juyi, 772–846; also called Lo-t’ien) was one of the great poets of the T’ang dynasty. Born in Shansi and raised in Honan, he passed the examinations in 800, served at court as a scholar of the Han-lin Academy and a censor, and was banished in 815 to Chiang-chou (Hsün-yang) on the Yangtze. Later he governed Hangchow and Soochow and ended his life in retirement at Lo-yang.

He wrote in a deliberately plain style, said to have been tested on an old peasant woman, and he used it for satires on injustice and for quiet poems on illness, idleness, friendship, wine, old age and the death of a small daughter. His close friend was the poet Yüan Chēn. His poetry was admired in Japan during his lifetime. Arthur Waley’s versions, from A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918) and More Translations from the Chinese (1919), are presented here in Waley’s spelling of the poet’s name.

poets.name: Homer
poets.credit: Portrait bust of Homer, Roman copy of a Hellenistic original — public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Homer is the name tradition gives to the poet, or poets, credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, the two foundational epics of ancient Greek literature. Nothing reliable is known of his life; ancient sources disagree even on his birthplace, and many scholars believe the poems as we have them are the culmination of centuries of oral epic tradition rather than the work of one man.

Whether historical individual or convenient legend, "Homer" is credited with shaping the Trojan War and the wanderings of Odysseus into the verse that became the bedrock of Greek and later Western literature and education.

This archive presents multiple English translations of the Iliad and the Odyssey side by side, so that the different choices each translator made — prose versus verse, plain diction versus ornate — can be compared directly.

poets.name: Sappho
poets.credit: Portrait bust of Sappho, Roman copy of a Greek original — public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Sappho was a Greek lyric poet from the island of Lesbos, active around the turn of the 7th to 6th century BC. Ancient critics ranked her among the very greatest poets; Plato is said to have called her the "Tenth Muse."

Almost none of her work survives complete. What remains — quotations in later grammarians, and a few papyrus scraps recovered from Egypt — comes down to us as fragments, some no more than a phrase, prized for their directness of feeling and technical mastery of the Aeolic dialect and sapphic metre.
The fragments gathered here follow Henry Thornton Wharton’s 1885 literal prose translation, the edition that first made Sappho’s surviving words accessible to English readers in their entirety.

poets.name: Anacreon
poets.credit: Statue of Anacreon from Monte Calvo, Roman copy (2nd century AD) after a Greek original, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Copenhagen; photograph by ChrisO, cropped · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anacreon of Teos (c. 582 – c. 485 BC) was an Ancient Greek lyric poet of the Ionian coast who spent his career at the courts of Polycrates of Samos and of the Pisistratid rulers of Athens. He was celebrated in antiquity for short, polished songs of wine, love and good company, and his name became a byword for the light-hearted drinking song.

Only fragments of his own verse survive. The poems traditionally printed as the Odes of Anacreon — the Anacreontea — are in fact, for the most part, later Greek imitations composed centuries after his death and handed down under his name. They were widely read and imitated in Renaissance and eighteenth-century Europe. These odes are given here in Thomas Moore’s free English verse translation of 1800, numbered I to LXXVIII as in his edition; the lengthy scholarly notes he printed with them are omitted.

poets.name: Virgil
poets.credit: Virgil enthroned between Clio and Melpomene, Roman mosaic from Hadrumetum (Bardo National Museum, Tunis), 3rd century AD · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Publius Vergilius Maro, known in English as Virgil, was born near Mantua in 70 BC and became the greatest poet of Augustan Rome. His Eclogues and the Georgics, a poem on farming and the countryside, made his name; his patron Maecenas brought him into the circle around the emperor Augustus.

The Aeneid, left unfinished at his death in 19 BC, tells how the Trojan prince Aeneas escapes the burning of Troy and carries his gods and his people to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. In twelve books it answers Homer in Latin and became the model for the Western epic. This archive presents it in John Dryden’s 1697 verse translation, in heroic couplets.

poets.name: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus)
poets.credit: Contorniate medallion with the head of Horace (late antique; Bibliotheque nationale de France, via Gallica), cropped · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Not a lifetime portrait: no ancient likeness of Horace survives.
bio: Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BC) was born at Venusia in southern Italy, the son of a freed slave. He was educated in Rome and Athens, fought on the losing side at Philippi (42 BC) under Brutus, and returned to Italy to find his family property confiscated. Through Virgil he met Maecenas, the great patron of the Augustan poets, who gave him a farm in the Sabine hills.

His Satires, Epodes, Odes and Epistles made him the leading lyric poet of Rome. The Odes, in four books, adapt the metres of the Greek lyricists Alcaeus and Sappho to Roman themes: wine and friendship, love, the brevity of life, the Augustan state. He also wrote the Carmen Saeculare for the Secular Games of 17 BC. The versions here are from John Conington's rhymed English translation of the Odes, which omits a few odes.

poets.name: Ovid
poets.credit: Portrait bust identified as Ovid — public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Publius Ovidius Naso, known as Ovid, was one of the leading poets of Augustan Rome, admired in his lifetime for his wit and technical fluency in Latin verse.

His masterwork, the Metamorphoses, is a sprawling narrative poem in fifteen books that retells hundreds of Greek and Roman myths of transformation, from the creation of the world to the deification of Julius Caesar. In AD 8 Augustus banished Ovid to Tomis on the Black Sea for reasons that remain unclear; he died there without returning to Rome.
This archive presents the Metamorphoses in Henry T. Riley’s 1851 prose translation, long a standard English rendering of the poem.

poets.name: Lucan
poets.credit: Portrait bust identified as Lucan — public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Marcus Annaeus Lucanus, known as Lucan, was a Roman poet born in Corduba (Córdoba, Spain) and raised in Rome, nephew of the philosopher Seneca the Younger.

His only surviving work, the Pharsalia (De Bello Civili), is an unfinished epic in ten books on the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey. Unusually for ancient epic, it dispenses with the gods entirely, focusing on human ambition and the collapse of the Roman Republic. Lucan fell out with the Emperor Nero, joined a conspiracy against him, and was forced to take his own life at twenty-five, reportedly reciting his own verses as he died.
This archive presents the Pharsalia in Sir Edward Ridley’s 1896 blank-verse translation.

poets.name: The Mu'allaqat Poets
poets.credit: The Holy Mosque at Mecca with the Kaaba, photograph by C. Snouck Hurgronje, 1889 (Bilder aus Mekka) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). No portraits of the poets exist; the Kaaba, on which the odes were said to be hung, stands in for them.
bio: The Mu'allaqat are seven long odes of pre-Islamic Arabia, composed in the sixth century by Imru' al-Qais, Tarafa, Zuhayr, Labid, Antara, Amr ibn Kulthum and al-Harith ibn Hilliza. The name means 'the suspended' or 'the hanged' poems: a later tradition held that they were embroidered in gold and hung on the Kaaba at Mecca. Many scholars doubt that story, but the odes remain the great monuments of classical Arabic poetry, opening with a lament at the abandoned campsite of the beloved and moving on to journeys, horses and camels, hunting, war and tribal pride.

This archive offers them in the English of Sir William Jones, first published in 1782 as The Moallakát and reprinted by W. A. Clouston in 1881. Jones renders the Arabic as prose, numbered verse by verse, rather than as English verse, much as Butler's Homer is prose; the site keeps his numbering, one verse to a line.

poets.name: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri
poets.credit: Imagined portrait by Kahlil Gibran (1917), no contemporary likeness exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri (973–1057) was a blind poet, philosopher and sceptic born in Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in northern Syria. Blinded by smallpox in childhood, he studied in Aleppo and Antioch, spent a short period in Baghdad, and returned to his home town, where he lived for decades as a celebrated ascetic and teacher, a vegetarian who called himself a prisoner of three things: blindness, solitude and the body. His verse questions revelation, priestly authority and the claims of every rival creed, and he has often been called the Voltaire or Lucretius of the Arabs.

His two great collections are Saqt al-zand (Sparks of the Tinder) and the Luzum ma la yalzam (The Necessity of What Is Not Necessary), the latter known as the Luzumiyat. The poems here are from Ameen Rihani's 1918 English version, a free rendering in quatrains selected from those books; they follow the sense and spirit of the Arabic rather than its form, which is monorhymed and in a different metre.

poets.name: Beowulf Poet
poets.credit: The Sutton Hoo helmet, c. early 7th century — an Anglo-Saxon warrior’s helmet contemporary with the world Beowulf describes; a symbolic image for this anonymous poet, not a portrait. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The author of Beowulf is unknown — an anonymous Anglo-Saxon poet whose single surviving epic, composed in Old English somewhere between the 8th and early 11th centuries, is the longest and most celebrated poem to survive from that period.

The poem survives in one manuscript, the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.xv), damaged by fire in 1731 and now held by the British Library. It tells of the Geatish hero Beowulf's battles with the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother, and, in old age, a dragon.

This text is the 1910 verse translation by the American philologist Francis Barton Gummere, prepared for the Harvard Classics and long in the public domain; it preserves the original's alliterative, four-stress line.

poets.name: Omar Khayyam
bio: Omar Khayyam (Ghiyath al-Din Abu'l-Fath Umar ibn Ibrahim al-Khayyam, 1048–1131) was a Persian mathematician, astronomer and philosopher born at Nishapur. He is remembered in the sciences for his work on cubic equations and for his part in reforming the Persian calendar, and in the West chiefly for the quatrains (ruba'iyat) attributed to him.

The English version here is E. H. Whinfield's 1883 translation, which he made from several Persian manuscripts and which numbers 500 quatrains. The attribution of many ruba'iyat to Omar is disputed, and scholars have long argued over which are genuinely his; the quatrains turn on wine, the tavern, the brevity of life and the mystical and sceptical questions of fate and faith. For Edward FitzGerald's celebrated freer rendering, already in this archive, see the poet FitzGerald.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old French)
poets.credit: Roland at Roncevaux: the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in eight stages, illumination by Simon Marmion from the Grandes Chroniques de France, 15th century (an illustration of the story, not a portrait; the poet is anonymous) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: The Chanson de Roland, the oldest major work of French literature, was composed in Old French around 1100 by a poet whose identity is unknown. It is a chanson de geste of some 4,000 lines in assonanced laisses, built on the defeat of Charlemagne's rearguard at Roncevaux in 778 and the vengeance that follows.

The earliest and best text survives in the Oxford manuscript, Digby 23, in the Bodleian Library, copied in Anglo-Norman England in the twelfth century. Its last line names a certain Turoldus ("Ci falt la geste que Turoldus declinet"), but whether he was the author, a copyist or a reciter has never been settled, and the poem is credited to no one with certainty.

poets.name: Anonymous (Old Norse)
poets.credit: A page of the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) — a manuscript page, not a portrait of any poet. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The mythological and heroic lays of the Old Norse tradition are anonymous. They were composed and handed down orally over several centuries, some of them perhaps as early as the 9th century, and were written down only in Iceland in the 13th. Their chief witness is the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to), an Icelandic manuscript copied around 1270 and rediscovered in the 17th century, which gathers most of the poems now known as the Poetic Edda; a few further lays survive in other manuscripts and in prose sagas.

The lays fall into two groups: poems of the gods, such as the Voluspo, the Hovamol and the Lokasenna, and poems of the heroes, such as the Volund, Helgi and Sigurth cycles and the lays of Guthrun and Atli. They are composed in short alliterative lines, often in speeches and dialogue, with brief prose links (kept in this archive) that supply the story between the verses. The collection is the principal source for Norse mythology and for the legends that later fed the Volsunga saga and the Nibelungenlied.

poets.name: Anonymous (Poem of the Cid)
poets.credit: The Tizona, the sword traditionally (though not verifiably) attributed to El Cid, now displayed at the Museum of Burgos — a symbolic image for this anonymous tradition, not a portrait. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: The medieval Spanish accounts of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, "El Cid" (c. 1043–1099), the Castilian warlord who became Spain’s national hero, were composed and compiled by unknown authors in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The great narrative poem on his exploits, the Cantar de Mio Cid, survives in a single incomplete manuscript and is itself anonymous.

This archive presents Robert Southey’s 1808 "Chronicle of the Cid," an English translation and compilation drawn chiefly from the medieval Crónica General de España together with other early chronicle and ballad material about the Cid — the fullest and best-known public-domain English account of the legend, though it is a prose chronicle rather than a verse rendering of the Cantar itself.

poets.name: Guido Cavalcanti
poets.credit: Imagined likeness, engraving from Rime (1813), no contemporary portrait exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Guido Cavalcanti (c. 1255–1300) was a Florentine poet and philosopher, the leading figure after Guinizzelli of the dolce stil novo, the 'sweet new style' of love poetry. Born into a wealthy Guelf family, he was drawn into the strife between the Black and White factions of Florence and was banished in 1300, spending his exile at Sarzana, where he fell ill; he returned to the city and died that same year. Dante called him his 'first friend' and dedicated the Vita Nuova to him.

His surviving verse, about fifty pieces, treats love as a dark, near-fatal force acting on the soul and its spirits, and is among the most intense of its age. The texts given here are Dante Gabriel Rossetti's English versions in The Early Italian Poets (1861), the translator's own selection of twenty-nine poems, which follow the Italian forms (sonnet, ballata and canzone) and rhyme patterns. Poems that Rossetti prints as the replies of other poets, and Dante's sonnets to Guido, are not included.

poets.name: Yunus Emre
bio: Yunus Emre is the first recorded native poet of the Western Turks: a mystic who wrote in Anatolian Turkish rather than in the Persian forms that Ottoman court poets later preferred. Ottoman biographers describe him as nearly unlettered, a disciple of the holy man Tapduk Emre, whose verse was held to be a direct gift of God.

Only a little is known of his life, and the early sources disagree. E. J. W. Gibb, whose History of Ottoman Poetry (1900) gives the first English account of him, notes that one of his own poems dates his devotion to the Path to the year 707 AH (1307–8), which places him about a century before the dates given by later biographers.

poets.name: Dante Alighieri
poets.credit: Portrait of Dante by Sandro Botticelli, c. 1495 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dante Alighieri was born in Florence in 1265 and became one of the city's political figures as well as its greatest poet. His early lyrics and the prose-and-verse Vita Nuova (c. 1294) celebrate Beatrice, the woman he loved from afar and who later became his guide in the Paradiso.

In 1302, on the losing side of Florence's factional struggles, he was sentenced to exile and never returned. During those years he wrote the Divine Comedy, a vision in rhymed tercets of the soul's journey through Hell, Purgatory and Heaven, composed in the Tuscan vernacular rather than Latin. He died in Ravenna in 1321, soon after finishing it.

poets.name: Anonymous (Middle English)
poets.credit: No portrait: these are the voices of unnamed singers and scribes, and no author’s name survives for any of them. They are known from manuscripts such as British Library Harley 978 (the ‘Cuckoo Song’), Harley 2253 (the Harley Lyrics) and Sloane 2593 (carols and songs).
bio: Most of the short poems that survive from medieval England carry no author’s name. They are songs, hymns, carols, ballads and charms, copied by clerks, friars and minstrels onto the spare leaves of larger books, and they reach us through a handful of manuscripts: the Reading Abbey volume that preserves ‘Sumer is icumen in’, the Harley miscellany (MS Harley 2253) with its love-songs and spring-songs, the song-book Sloane 2593 with its carols, and the Balliol commonplace book of Richard Hill, which holds ‘Lully, lulley’.

The poems gathered here run from about 1225 to the edge of the sixteenth century, with one later record of a far older custom. They include some of the earliest English love-songs, the plain and piercing carols of the fifteenth century, early ballads such as ‘Judas’ and ‘Robyn and Gandelyn’, the ‘Erthe upon erthe’ tradition of the memento mori, and the Yorkshire ‘Lyke-Wake Dirge’. The spelling is Middle English as the editors printed it.

poets.name: Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch)
poets.credit: Portrait of Francesco Petrarca (called Petrarch), French school, 17th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), known in English as Petrarch, was born in Arezzo to a Florentine notary exiled from his native city, and grew up in Avignon, then the seat of the papacy. He studied law at Montpellier and Bologna but gave himself to classical letters, recovering and copying Latin authors, and was crowned poet laureate on the Capitol in Rome in 1341. He spent his later years in northern Italy and died at Arquà, near Padua.

His Italian lyrics, the Rerum vulgarium fragmenta or Canzoniere, record his love for a woman named Laura, first seen in Avignon in 1327, whose death in 1348 divides the collection into poems written in her life and after her death. Their sonnet form and manner of address shaped European love poetry for centuries. The English versions here are from the 1879 Bohn volume, which prints several translations of most poems by different hands; the first version of each is given.

poets.name: Hafiz
poets.credit: Anselm Feuerbach, Hafis vor der Schenke (1852); an imagined likeness, as no contemporary portrait of Hafez exists · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Shams al-Din Muhammad Hafez of Shiraz (c. 1315–1390) is the most beloved lyric poet of Persia. He is remembered chiefly for his ghazals, short rhymed lyrics of love, wine and mystical longing, gathered after his death into the Divan. His pen-name, Hafiz, means one who has memorised the Qur'an. He lived in Shiraz, where his tomb remains a place of pilgrimage, and his verses are still consulted and recited across the Persian-speaking world.

The forty-three poems here are Gertrude Lowthian Bell's Poems from the Divan of Hafiz (London: Heinemann, 1897). They are free rhymed English versions rather than literal renderings, and Bell's own introduction and notes are left out.

poets.name: John Gower
poets.credit: Photograph of Gower's tomb effigy, Southwark Cathedral — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Gower (c. 1330–1408) was an English poet, a friend and contemporary of Chaucer, who wrote major long works in all three literary languages of his day: French (Mirour de l'Omme), Latin (Vox Clamantis), and English (Confessio Amantis).

A man of some property in Kent, he spent his later years at the Priory of St Mary Overie in Southwark, where his elaborate tomb, with its painted effigy resting its head on his three books, still stands in what is now Southwark Cathedral.

Confessio Amantis, his English masterwork, frames some hundred and forty tales as a lover's confession to a priest of Venus, moving through the Seven Deadly Sins toward a final meditation on age and the end of love — dedicated, in its first version, to Richard II.

poets.name: William Langland
poets.credit: No authenticated portrait of Langland survives; his very identity is a scholarly inference from the poem itself and a single manuscript note.
bio: William Langland is the name traditionally given to the presumed author of Piers Plowman, one of the great alliterative poems of medieval England, on the strength of a fifteenth-century manuscript note naming a “William de Langlond” as its maker.

Little is known of his life beyond what can be inferred from the poem: he seems to have received a clerical education, lived for a time in London, and moved in the world of minor clergy and the poor rather than the court.

Piers Plowman survives in three successive versions (the A, B, and C texts), which Langland appears to have revised and expanded over some twenty years. It follows a dreamer, Will, through a series of visions in search of Do-well, Do-bet, and Do-best — a sweeping allegorical satire of fourteenth-century church and society.

poets.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
poets.credit: Portrait of Geoffrey Chaucer (manuscript detail) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) was an English poet, civil servant, and diplomat, widely called the father of English poetry for demonstrating that the vernacular could carry the full weight of serious literary art.

He served in the royal household under three kings, worked as a customs official and clerk of the king's works, and travelled on diplomatic missions to France and Italy, where he likely encountered the work of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio.

His masterwork, The Canterbury Tales, left unfinished at his death, gathers a fellowship of pilgrims riding to Canterbury and telling stories in turn — a panorama of medieval English society in verse of astonishing variety and wit. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, in the corner that later became Poets' Corner.

poets.name: Gawain Poet
poets.credit: A page from the unique manuscript of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (British Library, Cotton Nero A.x) — a symbolic image for this anonymous poet, not a portrait. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
bio: Known also as the Pearl Poet, this anonymous author wrote in a north-west Midlands dialect of Middle English in the late fourteenth century, a contemporary of Chaucer working in a very different, alliterative tradition.

Four poems in a single surviving manuscript (British Library, Cotton Nero A.x) are usually attributed to this one poet on grounds of dialect, style, and shared concerns: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness (also called Purity). Nothing certain is known of the poet's identity.

Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, the best known of the four, is a chivalric romance and moral test of a Round Table knight, told with intricate structure and a rare sensitivity to the turning of the seasons.

poets.name: John Lydgate
poets.credit: Portrait of John Lydgate (illuminated manuscript) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Lydgate (c. 1370–c. 1451) was a Benedictine monk of Bury St Edmunds and, in his own lifetime, probably the most prolific and widely read poet in England — his surviving output runs to well over a hundred thousand lines.

He wrote in conscious imitation of Chaucer, whom he revered as his master, producing enormous works such as the Troy Book and the Fall of Princes alongside occasional verse, saints' lives, and courtly dream visions for patrons that included the royal house of Lancaster.
Modern taste has generally preferred Chaucer's economy to Lydgate's copiousness, but he was central to how English poetry was read and valued through the fifteenth century.

poets.name: Kabir
poets.credit: Kabir with a disciple, Company-school painting (c. 1825), an imagined likeness by an unknown artist · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Kabir was a Hindi-language mystic poet and weaver of Benares (Varanasi), traditionally dated c. 1440 to 1518. Born, by tradition, into a Muslim weaving family, he is said to have received initiation from the Hindu teacher Ramananda, and he rejected the claims of both Hindu and Muslim orthodoxy in favour of direct devotion to a single, formless God.

His short songs and couplets were transmitted orally and later collected in the Bijak, the Adi Granth of the Sikhs and other anthologies. The English Songs of Kabir (1915) were rendered by Rabindranath Tagore with the help of Evelyn Underhill, who wrote the introduction; this edition gives the hundred songs of that volume.

poets.name: William Dunbar
poets.credit: Portrait of William Dunbar — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Dunbar was a Scottish makar (court poet) attached to the household of King James IV, celebrated for the range and metrical virtuosity of his verse.
His poems move between satire, comic invective, and devotional lyric, and include the famous elegy ‘Lament for the Makers,’ with its refrain ‘Timor Mortis conturbat me.’

poets.name: John Skelton
poets.credit: Portrait of John Skelton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Skelton was an English poet and tutor to the young Prince Henry, later Henry VIII, remembered for the idiosyncratic short-lined verse form later called ‘Skeltonics.’
He wrote both courtly lyrics of praise and sharp satire of clergy and court, and was crowned poet laureate by three universities.

poets.name: Ludovico Ariosto
poets.credit: Portrait of Ludovico Ariosto, woodcut from the Ferrara edition of the Orlando Furioso (1532) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533) was born at Reggio Emilia and spent most of his life in the service of the Este family of Ferrara, first under Cardinal Ippolito d'Este and then, after 1517, under Duke Alfonso I. He wrote comedies and satires as well as lyrics, and was governor of the mountainous Garfagnana district for the duke from 1522 to 1525.

His masterpiece, the Orlando Furioso (first printed in 1516, revised in 1521 and again in the final edition of 1532), continues Boiardo's unfinished Orlando Innamorato in forty-six cantos of ottava rima. It weaves the madness of Orlando (Roland), the love of Ruggiero and Bradamante, and the war between Charlemagne and the Saracens into a single mock-heroic romance, and it deeply influenced Tasso, Spenser and later English poets. The version here is by William Stewart Rose, published in eight volumes by John Murray between 1823 and 1831.

poets.name: Stephen Hawes
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Stephen Hawes was an English poet who served as a groom of the chamber to Henry VII, best known for his allegorical romance ‘The Pastime of Pleasure.’
His verse bridges medieval allegory and the new humanism of the early Tudor court, and he was among the last English poets to write in the tradition of Chaucer and Lydgate.

poets.name: Michelangelo Buonarroti
poets.credit: Portrait of Michelangelo by Daniele da Volterra (c. 1545) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564) was born at Caprese in Tuscany and trained in Florence. He is remembered above all as a sculptor, painter and architect, of the David, the Sistine Chapel ceiling and the dome of St Peter’s, but he also wrote poetry throughout his long life, working at madrigals and sonnets in the Tuscan tradition of Dante and Petrarch.

His surviving verse, about three hundred poems, was not published as a book in his lifetime. It speaks of beauty, love and art, of his friendships with Tommaso de’ Cavalieri and Vittoria Colonna, and, in old age, of death and the longing for God. This selection is John Addington Symonds’s rhymed English version of 1878; where Michelangelo left two versions of a sonnet, both are given.

poets.name: Fuzuli
bio: Fuzuli (Mehmed bin Süleyman, c. 1483–1556) was one of the greatest poets of the sixteenth-century Turkish world. He wrote in Azerbaijani Turkish, Ottoman Turkish, Persian and Arabic, and is remembered above all for his romance Leyla and Mejnun, the tale of the lover driven mad by his love for Leyla.

E. J. W. Gibb, whose Ottoman Poems (1882) gives the first English translations of his ghazels, noted that Fuzuli's Leyla and Mejnun contains many touching passages of great beauty. The poems below are from that volume.

poets.name: Sir Thomas Wyatt
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Thomas Wyatt — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Thomas Wyatt was a Kentish courtier and diplomat under Henry VIII, credited with introducing the sonnet form into English poetry after his travels in Italy.
His lyrics of love and court intrigue circulated in manuscript during his lifetime and were first printed posthumously in Tottel’s Miscellany (1557).

poets.name: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, was an English nobleman and poet who, alongside his friend Sir Thomas Wyatt, helped pioneer the English sonnet and was the first to write English verse in blank verse.
He was executed for treason in the last weeks of Henry VIII’s reign, at the age of twenty-nine.

poets.name: Luís de Camões
poets.credit: Portrait of Luís de Camões, attributed to Fernão Gomes (16th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Luís Vaz de Camões was a Portuguese poet, widely regarded as the greatest in the Portuguese language. He served in the Portuguese enterprises in North Africa and the East, losing the sight of one eye in battle at Ceuta, and spent many years abroad in India and Macao before returning to Lisbon.

His epic Os Lusíadas, published in 1572, celebrates Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and the history of the Portuguese people in ten cantos of ottava rima. He is also remembered for his lyric poetry, and died in Lisbon in 1580. This archive holds Sir Richard Francis Burton's English version of the epic, published in 1880.

poets.name: George Gascoigne
poets.credit: Portrait of George Gascoigne — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Gascoigne was an English soldier, courtier and poet whose ‘A Hundreth Sundrie Flowres’ (1573) is considered one of the first substantial collections of original English verse and prose.
He also wrote what is often called the first original prose comedy in English and an early treatise on the art of English versification.

poets.name: Torquato Tasso
poets.credit: Portrait of Torquato Tasso aged 22 by Jacopo Bassano (c. 1566) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Torquato Tasso (1544–1595) was an Italian poet born at Sorrento, the son of the courtier-poet Bernardo Tasso. He studied at Padua and Bologna and from the 1560s served the Este court at Ferrara, where he wrote the pastoral play Aminta (1573) and worked for years on his epic of the First Crusade.

Gerusalemme liberata (Jerusalem Delivered), first published in 1581, tells of the Christian siege of Jerusalem under Godfrey of Bouillon and became one of the most influential epics of the late Renaissance. Tasso suffered long periods of mental distress and confinement in the 1570s and 1580s, and later revised the poem as Gerusalemme conquistata. He died in Rome in 1595. Edward Fairfax's English version appeared in 1600.

poets.name: Alexander Montgomerie
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Montgomerie — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Montgomerie was a Scottish Jacobean courtier and makar, master poet at the court of James VI, best known for the allegorical dream-poem ‘The Cherrie and the Slae.’
A Catholic at a Protestant court, he later fell from royal favour over his religion and political dealings.

poets.name: Nicholas Breton
poets.credit: Portrait of Nicholas Breton — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nicholas Breton was a prolific English poet and prose writer of the Elizabethan and Jacobean periods, admired for pastoral lyrics such as ‘Phillida and Coridon.’
He wrote across a remarkable range of genres, from devotional verse to satire, over a career of some fifty years.

poets.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Walter Raleigh — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Walter Raleigh was an English courtier, explorer and poet, a favourite of Elizabeth I who later fell from favour and was ultimately executed under James I.
His surviving poems, several written while imprisoned in the Tower of London, meditate with stoic clarity on time, fortune and mortality.

poets.name: Edmund Spenser
poets.credit: Portrait of Edmund Spenser — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Spenser was an English poet best known for his epic ‘The Faerie Queene,’ but he also wrote a substantial body of shorter verse, including the pastoral ‘Shepheardes Calender,’ the sonnet sequence ‘Amoretti,’ and the wedding hymns ‘Epithalamion’ and ‘Prothalamion.’
He spent much of his career in Ireland as a colonial administrator, and his poetry stands at the centre of English Renaissance literature.

poets.name: Thomas Lodge
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Thomas Lodge was an English poet, dramatist and prose romancer whose pastoral romance ‘Rosalynde’ (1590) later supplied Shakespeare with the plot of ‘As You Like It.’
His lyric poems, many embedded as songs within his prose fictions, are prized for their musicality and pastoral grace.

poets.name: Robert Greene
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Greene — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Greene was an Elizabethan playwright, pamphleteer and poet, notorious in his own time for his dissolute life and for a posthumous pamphlet often read as an attack on the young William Shakespeare.
His lyric poems, many sung by characters in his prose romances, are notable for their pastoral grace and simplicity.

poets.name: Robert Southwell
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Southwell — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Southwell was an English Jesuit priest and poet who was arrested, tortured and executed for treason under Elizabeth I because of his underground Catholic ministry.
His devotional verse, most famously ‘The Burning Babe,’ was admired even by contemporaries hostile to his faith.

poets.name: Thomas Campion
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Campion — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Campion was an English composer, physician and poet who wrote and set to music his own delicate, classically influenced lyrics.
He also published a treatise arguing for quantitative, unrhymed verse in English, though his own most enduring songs are rhymed airs.

poets.name: Tommaso Campanella
poets.credit: Portrait of Tommaso Campanella by Francesco Cozza (17th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Tommaso Campanella (1568–1639) was a Calabrian Dominican friar, philosopher and poet. He was imprisoned by the Spanish authorities in Naples for twenty-seven years after a failed conspiracy against Spanish rule in 1599, and wrote much of his philosophy, including the utopia The City of the Sun, in prison.

His Italian poems, the Scelta d’alcune poesie filosofiche, mix metaphysics, political protest and religious prophecy in sonnets and canzoni. They were first published in Germany in 1622. This selection of his sonnets is John Addington Symonds’s rhymed English version of 1878.

poets.name: Sir John Davies
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Davies was an English poet, lawyer and politician who later served as Attorney General for Ireland.
He is best remembered for ‘Nosce Teipsum,’ a long philosophical poem on the nature of the soul, and for witty, compact epigrams on the paradox of human self-knowledge.

poets.name: Richard Barnfield
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Richard Barnfield was an English poet whose pastoral and erotic verse, including ‘The Affectionate Shepherd,’ was controversial in its own time for its open homoeroticism.
Some of his lyrics, including ‘As it fell upon a day,’ were long misattributed to his contemporary William Shakespeare.

poets.name: Christopher Marlowe
poets.credit: Portrait of Christopher Marlowe — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christopher Marlowe (1564-1593) was an English poet and dramatist, the most celebrated of the University Wits and the leading figure of Elizabethan tragedy before Shakespeare.

Alongside his plays he left a body of non-dramatic verse, including the unfinished mythological poem Hero and Leander and a translation of Ovid's Amores, and was killed in a Deptford tavern brawl at twenty-nine.

poets.name: William Shakespeare
poets.credit: Portrait of William Shakespeare — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) was an English poet and playwright from Stratford-upon-Avon, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language.
Beyond his plays, his non-dramatic verse includes the 154 Sonnets, the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece, and the shorter pieces collected as The Passionate Pilgrim.

poets.name: Ben Jonson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ben Jonson — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ben Jonson (1572-1637) was an English poet and playwright, the dominant literary figure of the Jacobean stage and a rival and friend of Shakespeare.

Beyond his comedies and tragedies, he wrote a substantial body of lyric and occasional verse, including epigrams and elegies collected here from a posthumous volume of his poems and prose "Discoveries."

poets.name: Sir Philip Sidney
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir Philip Sidney · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir Philip Sidney (1554–1586) was an English poet, courtier, and soldier, killed at the Battle of Zutphen at thirty-one.
His sonnet sequence Astrophel and Stella (1591) is the first great sequence in English, chronicling an unrequited, thinly-veiled autobiographical love.

poets.name: Fulke Greville
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Fulke Greville, Lord Brooke (1554–1628), was an English poet and statesman, the close friend and biographer of Philip Sidney.
His philosophical sequences, published posthumously as Certaine Learned and Elegant Workes, weigh monarchy, religion, and human frailty in dense, difficult verse.

poets.name: Samuel Daniel
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Samuel Daniel (1562–1619) was an English poet and historian, admired for the plain, measured elegance of his style.
His sonnet sequence Delia and the narrative poem The Complaint of Rosamond made his early reputation.

poets.name: Michael Drayton
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Michael Drayton (1563–1631) was an English poet whose vast body of work spans the sonnet sequence Idea, historical verse, and the topographical epic Poly-Olbion.
His Barons' Wars retells the civil strife of Edward II's reign in stately ottava rima.

poets.name: William Drummond of Hawthornden
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Drummond of Hawthornden (1585–1649) was the first considerable Scottish poet to write in English rather than Scots.
His polished sonnets and elegies were shaped by his wide reading in French and Italian verse.

poets.name: John Donne
poets.credit: Portrait of John Donne by Isaac Oliver · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Donne (1572–1631) was an English poet and cleric, the foremost of the metaphysical poets.
His verse — by turns erotic, witty, and devout — moved from the love poems of his youth to the religious sonnets of his years as Dean of St Paul's.

poets.name: George Herbert
poets.credit: Portrait of George Herbert · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Herbert (1593–1633) was a Welsh-born English poet and priest, a central figure of the metaphysical school.
His single collection, The Temple (1633), published just after his death, gathers the devotional lyrics for which he is loved.

poets.name: Thomas Carew
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of Carew survives.
bio: Thomas Carew (1595–1640) was an English Cavalier poet at the court of Charles I, admired for the polish of his amorous lyrics.
His Poems (1640) circulated widely and shaped the courtly style later followed by Lovelace and Suckling.

poets.name: Sir John Suckling
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Suckling (1609–1641) was an English Cavalier poet and courtier, famed for his wit and his invention of the card game cribbage.
His collected verse, Fragmenta Aurea (1646), mixes light, conversational love lyrics with plays and prose.

poets.name: Nathaniel Whiting
poets.credit: No portrait of Whiting is known.
bio: Nathaniel Whiting was a Cambridge-educated poet and later a Puritan minister. He took his B.A. at Queens' College, Cambridge, in 1631 and his M.A. in 1635, and in 1637 published, under the initials N. W., the long verse romance Le Hore di Recreatione, or The Pleasant History of Albino and Bellama. He later became minister of Aldwincle in Northamptonshire and was deprived of the living at the Restoration.

Albino and Bellama, printed with the dream-poem Il Insonio Insonnadado that defends poetry against its critics, is written in an odd, inventive diction. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921).

poets.name: Sir William Davenant
poets.credit: Portrait of Sir William Davenant · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sir William Davenant (1606–1668) was an English poet and playwright who served as Poet Laureate from 1638. A bridge between the ages of Shakespeare and Dryden, he helped reopen and reshape the English theatre after the Restoration.
His most ambitious work is the unfinished heroic poem Gondibert (1651); the collection Madagascar; with Other Poems (1638) gathers his courtly and occasional verse.

poets.name: Henry King
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Henry King (1592–1669) was an English poet and Bishop of Chichester.
He is remembered above all for ‘The Exequy,’ his elegy for his young wife — one of the great grief poems of the century.

poets.name: John Milton
poets.credit: Portrait, Christ’s College, Cambridge · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and polemicist, author of the epic Paradise Lost. He went blind in mid-life and composed his greatest work by dictation.
Though he predates the Romantic movement, his blank verse and his figure of Satan shaped nearly every English poet who followed.

poets.name: Richard Crashaw
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of Crashaw survives.
bio: Richard Crashaw (1613–1649) was an English metaphysical poet known for the ecstatic, ornate devotion of his sacred verse.
A convert to Catholicism, he collected his poems as Steps to the Temple (1646), consciously following George Herbert.

poets.name: John Cleveland
poets.credit: Engraved portrait of John Cleveland, frontispiece to his Works (1687) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Cleveland (1613–1658) was an English Royalist poet and satirist, a fellow of St John's College, Cambridge, who lost his post when the Civil War came and served the King's cause with his pen. He is best known for his sharp political satires against Scots, Parliament men and Puritans, and for love poems in the most extravagant 'strong-lined' conceited style.

Cleveland's verse was enormously popular in the 1650s and was reprinted many times, though the collections that carry his name also contain pieces by other hands. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921), using the poems he prints as Cleveland's and leaving out those he marks as disputed.

poets.name: Abraham Cowley
poets.credit: Portrait of Abraham Cowley by Sir Peter Lely · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Abraham Cowley (1618–1667) was among the most celebrated English poets of his century, a child prodigy admired for his metaphysical wit.
His 1656 Poems gathers odes, elegies, and the love sequence The Mistress.

poets.name: Richard Lovelace
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait of this collection's engraving survives in the public record used here.
bio: Richard Lovelace (1617–1657) was an English Cavalier poet who fought and was imprisoned for the Royalist cause.
Best remembered for ‘To Althea, from Prison’ and ‘To Lucasta, Going to the Wars,’ his posthumous Lucasta volumes appeared in 1659.

poets.name: William Habington
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: William Habington (1605–1654) was an English poet whose single collection, Castara (1634), celebrates — unusually for the age — his courtship and marriage to one woman.

poets.name: Sir John Denham
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir John Denham (1615–1669) was an English poet best known for Cooper's Hill (1642), a landscape meditation that founded the English topographical poem.
His couplets were much admired by Dryden and Pope for their balance and control.

poets.name: Thomas Randolph
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Randolph · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Randolph (1605–1635) was an English poet and dramatist, a celebrated wit at Cambridge and an adopted ‘son’ of Ben Jonson.
He died at twenty-nine; his collected Poems appeared three years later.

poets.name: Edmund Waller
poets.credit: Portrait of Edmund Waller · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edmund Waller (1606–1687) was an English poet and politician whose smooth, regular couplets influenced the coming Augustan style.
He wrote equally fluent verse for both sides of the Civil War, a flexibility that shadowed his reputation.

poets.name: Sir Charles Sedley
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Sir Charles Sedley (1639–1701) was an English Restoration poet, playwright, and courtier known for his wit and libertine reputation at the court of Charles II.

poets.name: George Wither
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: George Wither (1588–1667) was a prolific English poet and pamphleteer whose early verse, collected as Juvenilia, made him one of the most popular poets of his generation before his turn to satire and religious controversy.

poets.name: Robert Herrick
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Herrick · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Herrick (1591–1674) was an English poet and clergyman, the most prolific of the Cavalier poets.
His single vast collection, Hesperides (1648), moves between pagan celebration, courtly love, and country ritual — over a thousand short poems in one book.

poets.name: Andrew Marvell
poets.credit: Portrait of Andrew Marvell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Marvell (1621–1678) was an English metaphysical poet and politician.
Celebrated for lyrics such as ‘To His Coy Mistress’ and ‘The Garden,’ most of his poems appeared posthumously in the Miscellaneous Poems of 1681.

poets.name: Jean de La Fontaine
poets.credit: Portrait of Jean de La Fontaine by Hyacinthe Rigaud, 1690 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695) was a French poet born at Château-Thierry in Champagne. After an unsettled early career in law and the administration of forests and waters, he found patrons in Paris, among them Nicolas Fouquet and later Madame de La Sablière, and became one of the glories of the age of Louis XIV; he was elected to the Académie française in 1684.

His Fables, published in collected books between 1668 and 1694, retell the stories of Aesop, Phaedrus and the Indian tradition in supple, irregular verse of great wit and economy. Under the guise of animals they observe the manners, vanities and cruelties of court and town. This selection follows the English verse translation by Walter Thornbury (London, 1886), printed with Gustave Doré's illustrations.

poets.name: Henry Vaughan
poets.credit: Title-page emblem from Silex Scintillans (1650) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Vaughan (1621–1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet and physician who styled himself ‘the Silurist.’
He is best known for the sacred poems of Silex Scintillans (1650), written under the deep influence of George Herbert.

poets.name: Thomas Stanley
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Stanley, 1660 · Public domain (Wikipedia)
bio: Thomas Stanley (1625–1678) was an English poet, translator and scholar, remembered for his History of Philosophy (1655–62) and for his edition of Aeschylus. Educated at Cambridge, he lived in London and moved among Royalist writers such as Shirley and Fanshawe.

His own poems, first printed in 1647 and reprinted in 1651 and 1656, are polished, graceful love lyrics addressed mostly to a lady called Chariessa or Celia. This selection takes his original poems from George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921) and leaves out the pieces that Stanley translated from other poets.

poets.name: Katherine Philips
poets.credit: Portrait of Katherine Philips · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Katherine Philips (1632–1664), called ‘the Matchless Orinda,’ was an English poet and translator.
She was admired above all for her poems of female friendship; her collected Poems appeared in 1664 and 1667.

poets.name: John Dryden
poets.credit: Portrait of John Dryden by an unknown artist, after Sir Godfrey Kneller · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Dryden (1631–1700) was England’s dominant literary figure of the later 17th century — poet, satirist, playwright, and critic — and was made the first official Poet Laureate in 1668.
His satires — Absalom and Achitophel, Mac Flecknoe, The Medal — and his public odes set the model for Augustan verse that Pope and Swift would inherit.

poets.name: Thomas Flatman
poets.credit: Thomas Flatman, self-portrait miniature · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Flatman (1635–1688) was an English poet and miniature painter, born in London, educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford, and called to the bar at the Inner Temple. He became a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1668 and was admired for his portrait miniatures as much as for his verse.

His Poems and Songs went through four editions between 1674 and 1686. They range from Pindaric odes on the deaths of public figures, through devotional pieces such as the Hymn for the Morning, to witty songs and satires. The text here follows George Saintsbury's Minor Poets of the Caroline Period, vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921), leaving out his Latin pieces and his translations and paraphrases of Horace, Ovid and others.

poets.name: Köroğlu
bio: Köroğlu (Kurroglou in older English spellings) is the legendary bandit-poet of Turkish and Turkic folklore. He robbed the caravans on the road between Persia and the Ottoman lands, and is remembered above all for the improvised songs he is said to have sung. He is the hero of a large cycle of tales and songs carried by wandering minstrels among the Turkic peoples of Anatolia, Azerbaijan and Central Asia.

The cycle is traditional, and its authorship is not known: no single author can be named, and the songs were passed on orally and changed with each telling. The English version used here is from Alexander Chodzko's Specimens of the Popular Poetry of Persia (1842), which places the hero in northern Khorasan in the second half of the seventeenth century. Chodzko's versions are set within his prose narrative, so the songs are given as paragraphs rather than as verse lines.

poets.name: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea
bio: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea (1661–1720), née Kingsmill, was a maid of honour to Mary of Modena and married Heneage Finch in 1684. After the Revolution of 1688 the couple retired to the country, where she wrote most of her poems. She published Miscellany Poems, on Several Occasions in 1713 and often called herself Ardelia in her verse.

Her ‘Nocturnal Reverie’ was singled out by Wordsworth as a rare piece of fresh nature description in its century, and her ode ‘The Spleen’ is among the earliest English poems on melancholy as a condition. She also wrote fables, satires, songs and religious poems.

poets.name: Matthew Prior
bio: Matthew Prior (1664–1721) was the son of a joiner, educated at Westminster School and Cambridge, and made his career as a diplomat. He served as secretary to the embassy at The Hague and in Paris, and took part in the negotiations that led to the Treaty of Utrecht, and was imprisoned for a time after the Whig ministry came to power in 1715.

As a poet he was admired for his light, polished verse: songs and epigrams addressed to Cloe, tales and fables, and longer poems such as Alma and Solomon. His Poems on Several Occasions was published by subscription in 1718.

poets.name: Jonathan Swift
poets.credit: Portrait of Jonathan Swift by Charles Jervas, c. 1718 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jonathan Swift (1667–1745), Dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin, is remembered above all for his prose satires, but his verse — plain-spoken, often savage, sometimes tender — was equally his own invention.

Poems like A Description of a City Shower and The Lady’s Dressing-Room turned unflinching, unglamorous observation into satire, while Cadenus and Vanessa and the Stella poems show a gentler, more private side of a famously guarded man.

poets.name: Nedim
bio: Ahmed Nedim was one of the most celebrated Ottoman poets of the early 18th century, the age later called the Tulip Era, a period of peace, luxury and garden-pavilion culture in Istanbul. He wrote the courtly ghazel and became librarian and boon-companion of the Grand Vezir Ibrahim Pasha.

He died in October 1730, when the palace was stormed in the uprising that overthrew Sultan Ahmed III. E. J. W. Gibb, whose History of Ottoman Poetry gives the first sustained English account of him, warned that Nedim's delicate verbal music could scarcely survive translation. The poems below are Gibb's renderings of ghazels from the fourth volume of that history.

poets.name: Edward Young
bio: Edward Young (1683–1765) was born in Hampshire and educated at Oxford, where he became a fellow of All Souls. He made his name with a poem on the Last Judgment, a series of satires called The Love of Fame, and some tragedies, and took holy orders in middle age, becoming rector of Welwyn in Hertfordshire in 1730.

His blank-verse The Complaint, or Night Thoughts (1742–1745), a long meditation in nine Nights on life, death and immortality, was one of the most widely read poems in Europe in the later eighteenth century. William Blake made a famous series of designs for it.

poets.name: John Gay
bio: John Gay (1685–1732) was an English poet and dramatist, born in Barnstaple, Devon. A friend of Pope, Swift and Arbuthnot, he wrote Trivia, a mock-georgic on walking the streets of London, and The Beggar’s Opera (1728), a ballad opera that was a great popular success.

His Fables, published in two series in 1727 and 1738, are short verse stories in which animals speak and act as foils to human folly. They were widely read for generations and are the part of his verse that still has readers.

poets.name: Alexander Pope
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Pope by Michael Dahl, c. 1727 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Pope (1688–1744) was the foremost English poet of the early 18th century, master of the heroic couplet and the sharpest satirist of his age.

Barred by his Catholicism and ill health from university or public office, he made a career (and a fortune) from his verse and his acclaimed translation of Homer; The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man remain his best-loved works.

poets.name: Robert Blair
bio: Robert Blair (1699–1746) was a Scottish minister and poet, born in Edinburgh and for many years parish minister of Athelstaneford in East Lothian. He wrote little verse that survives.

His blank-verse poem The Grave (1743) is a gloomy meditation on death and the churchyard in the manner of the so-called graveyard poets, and was often reprinted, notably with William Blake’s designs in 1808.

poets.name: Samuel Johnson
poets.credit: Portrait of Samuel Johnson by Sir Joshua Reynolds, c. 1772 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784) — lexicographer, essayist, critic, and the dominant literary figure of mid-18th-century England — also wrote poetry of severe, weighty moral force.
London and The Vanity of Human Wishes, both close imitations of Juvenal’s satires, and his plain elegy for his friend Robert Levet, show the same unflinching realism that marks his prose.

poets.name: Mikhail Lomonosov
poets.credit: Portrait of Mikhail Lomonosov, engraving by L. Miropolsky (1787) after Georg Caspar Prenner · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Mikhail Vasilyevich Lomonosov (1711–1765) was born near Kholmogory in the far north of Russia, the son of a fisherman. He studied in Moscow and in Germany, became a professor at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, took part in founding Moscow University (1755), and worked as both scientist and poet. He helped fix the rules of Russian versification and the literary language, and his solemn odes made him the leading Russian poet of the mid-eighteenth century.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Thomas Gray
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Gray by John Giles Eccardt, 1747-48 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Gray (1716–1771) was a reclusive Cambridge scholar who published only a handful of poems in his lifetime, yet his Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard became one of the most quoted poems in the English language.
His Pindaric odes The Progress of Poesy and The Bard helped carry English verse from Augustan restraint toward the Romantic sublime.

poets.name: Mark Akenside
bio: Mark Akenside (1721–1770) was born in Newcastle upon Tyne, the son of a butcher, and studied at Edinburgh and Leiden before practising as a physician in London. He was lame from a boyhood accident.

His blank-verse The Pleasures of Imagination (1744), a philosophical poem on the sources of aesthetic pleasure, made him famous when he was in his early twenties, and he later reworked it at length. His Odes and Hymn to the Naiads share its classical models and its enthusiasm for liberty.

poets.name: William Collins
bio: William Collins (1721–1759) was born in Chichester and educated at Winchester and Oxford. He went to London to live by his pen, and his small output of odes, published in 1746, made little stir at first but is now ranked among the finest lyric poetry of the century.

His odes to Evening, Fear and Simplicity, and ‘How sleep the brave,’ are often seen as turning eighteenth-century verse toward feeling and imagination. His mind failed in his later years and he died in Chichester at thirty-seven.

poets.name: Christopher Smart
bio: Christopher Smart (1722–1771) was born in Kent and educated at Cambridge, where he became a fellow of Pembroke Hall. He lived in London as a hack writer and was confined for mental illness between 1756 and 1763. He died in a debtors’ prison.

His A Song to David (1763) is the poem by which he is chiefly remembered; its ecstatic language was thought a sign of his madness and it was little read for a century. His Hymns for the Amusement of Children appeared in 1771, and Jubilate Agno, written in confinement, was not published until the twentieth century.

poets.name: Oliver Goldsmith
poets.credit: Portrait of Oliver Goldsmith after Sir Joshua Reynolds · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Goldsmith (1728–1774) was an Irish-born writer of extraordinary range — poet, playwright, and novelist — whose warmth and clarity made him one of the best-loved authors of his age.
The Deserted Village, his elegy for a vanishing rural England, and Retaliation, his affectionate mock-epitaphs on his own dinner-table friends, remain his most-read poems.

poets.name: William Cowper
poets.credit: Portrait of William Cowper by Lemuel Francis Abbott, 1792 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Cowper (1731–1800) wrote from a life shadowed by recurring breakdowns and religious despair, retired to the Buckinghamshire village of Olney under the care of friends.

His comic ballad John Gilpin made him briefly famous, but his lasting achievement is The Task, a long meditative poem on rural retirement, and the Olney Hymns he wrote with John Newton, including “God Moves in a Mysterious Way.”

poets.name: Vasily Petrov
bio: Vasily Petrovich Petrov (1736–1799), born in Moscow, was a court poet under Catherine II. He wrote ceremonial odes on Russian victories and translated Virgil’s Aeneid into Russian verse.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Anna Seward
poets.credit: Portrait of Anna Seward by Tilly Kettle (1762) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Anna Seward (1742–1809), born at Eyam in Derbyshire and raised in Lichfield, where her father was a canon of the cathedral, was known in her own day as the “Swan of Lichfield”. She was educated at home on progressive lines and became a prominent figure in the literary society of the Midlands, publishing an elegy on Captain Cook, a monody on Major André and the poetical novel Louisa (1784).

Her Original Sonnets on Various Subjects, and Odes Paraphrased from Horace appeared in 1799. The hundred sonnets, many in the Petrarchan and Miltonic manner and some of them nature poems or elegies, helped to revive the English sonnet in the years before Wordsworth, and the Horatian paraphrases freely expand their originals. Her letters were published posthumously in 1811.

poets.name: Ippolit Bogdanovich
bio: Ippolit Fyodorovich Bogdanovich (1743–1803), of Ukrainian origin, served as a state official and wrote light, graceful verse. His best-known work is Dushenka (1783), a free adaptation of La Fontaine’s tale of Psyche, which earned him Bowring’s title of “the Russian Anacreon”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Anna Laetitia Barbauld
bio: Anna Laetitia Barbauld (1743–1825), née Aikin, was born in Leicestershire, the daughter of a Dissenting minister and schoolmaster, and grew up at Warrington Academy. Her Poems (1773) went through several editions within a year, and she went on to write hymns, children’s books and essays and to teach at a school she ran with her husband.

Her later work includes the long political poem Eighteen Hundred and Eleven (1812), which looks forward to the decline of Britain and the rise of America. She was a friend of Joseph Priestley and a figure in the Dissenting and literary circles of her day.

poets.name: Gavrila Derzhavin
poets.credit: Portrait of Gavrila Derzhavin by Vladimir Borovikovsky (1811) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gavrila Romanovich Derzhavin (1743–1816), born near Kazan, served as a soldier and then as a state official: secretary to Catherine II, governor of provinces, and later Minister of Justice. His odes “Felitsa” (1782) and “God” (1784) brought him fame, and he is usually counted the greatest Russian poet before Pushkin. “God” was translated into many languages, and Bowring’s version of it is among the best known in English.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Ivan Khemnitser
bio: Ivan Ivanovich Khemnitser (1745–1784), of German descent, was a mining engineer and later a Russian consul in Smyrna, where he died. He is remembered for his fables, first published in 1779, whose plain, humorous style set an example for Krylov.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
poets.credit: Portrait of Goethe by Joseph Karl Stieler (1828) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was born in Frankfurt am Main and studied law before the success of his novel The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774) made him famous across Europe. In 1775 he moved to Weimar at the invitation of Duke Karl August, where he served as a minister of state and director of the court theatre, and from 1794 he was the close friend and collaborator of Friedrich Schiller.

Best known for the drama Faust, he wrote lyrics, ballads, odes, elegies and epigrams throughout his life, from the early songs and the Roman Elegies and Venetian Epigrams of his Italian years to the West-Eastern Divan (1819), inspired by the Persian poet Hafiz. The English versions here are from Edgar Alfred Bowring’s 1853 The Poems of Goethe, translated in the original metres; it is a selection from his shorter verse.

poets.name: Charlotte Smith
poets.credit: Portrait of Charlotte Smith by George Romney (1792) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charlotte Smith (1749–1806) was an English poet and novelist, born Charlotte Turner and raised in Sussex and Surrey. Married young to a spendthrift husband who was imprisoned for debt in 1783, she turned to writing to support her many children.

Her Elegiac Sonnets (1784), expanded through many editions, is often credited with reviving the English sonnet as a form for personal feeling, and its melancholy landscapes of the Sussex downs and coast lie behind much Romantic poetry. She was also a successful novelist, and her long blank-verse poem Beachy Head appeared after her death in 1807.

poets.name: Phillis Wheatley
bio: Phillis Wheatley (c. 1753–1784) was born in West Africa, kidnapped and brought to Boston as a child in 1761, and purchased by the merchant John Wheatley. Taught to read and write in his household, she began publishing verse as a teenager.

Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773) was the first book of poems published by an African American. A group of Boston notables attested in its front matter that she had written the poems; she was freed shortly after the book appeared.

poets.name: Thomas Chatterton
bio: Thomas Chatterton (1752–1770) was born in Bristol, the posthumous son of a schoolmaster and church official, and was writing remarkable verse before he was in his teens. He invented a fifteenth-century Bristol priest named Thomas Rowley and wrote a body of poems in an imitation medieval English, passing them off as Rowley's recovered manuscripts.

He went to London in 1770 hoping to live by his pen and died there in August of that year, aged seventeen. The question whether the Rowley poems were genuine was argued for decades, but they are now known to be his own. Wordsworth called him ‘the marvellous Boy,’ and Keats dedicated Endymion to his memory.

poets.name: Yury Neledinsky-Meletsky
bio: Yury Aleksandrovich Neledinsky-Meletsky (1752–1828) was a court official who served under Catherine II and Paul I. He is remembered for songs written in the manner of Russian folk lyrics, many of which were set to music and sung widely.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: George Crabbe
bio: George Crabbe (1754–1832) was born at Aldeburgh on the Suffolk coast, trained as a surgeon and apothecary, and went to London in 1780 to try his fortune as a poet. Edmund Burke took him up, and he afterward became a clergyman. The Village (1783), which Samuel Johnson read in manuscript, set out to show the real life of the rural poor against the conventions of pastoral.

His later narrative poems, The Parish Register, The Borough and the Tales, tell the lives of ordinary people in plain, exact couplets and were widely read in his day. Peter Grimes, from The Borough, is the source of Benjamin Britten’s opera.

poets.name: Yermil Kostrov
bio: Yermil Ivanovich Kostrov (1755–1796) studied at Moscow University and made a name as a translator. He rendered part of Homer’s Iliad into Russian verse and worked on a version of Ossian, which, as Bowring notes, was completed after his early death by Gnedich.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: William Blake
poets.credit: Portrait by Thomas Phillips (1807) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Blake (1757–1827) was an English poet, painter, and printmaker, largely unrecognised in his lifetime and now seen as a seminal figure of the Romantic age.
He engraved and hand-coloured his own illuminated books, most famously Songs of Innocence and of Experience, where word and image are inseparable.

poets.name: Mikhail Muravyov
bio: Mikhail Nikitich Muravyov (1757–1807) was a poet and teacher who served as tutor to the future Alexander I and later as a curator of Moscow University. His gentle, personal verse looked forward to the sentimental school of Karamzin and Zhukovsky.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Vasily Kapnist
bio: Vasily Vasilyevich Kapnist (1758–1823), of Greek-Ukrainian family, wrote odes, songs and the satirical comedy Chicane (1798). Bowring notes that he wrote “on a variety of subjects”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Robert Burns
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Burns by Alexander Nasmyth, 1787 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Burns (1759–1796), Scotland’s national poet, turned the everyday life and speech of Ayrshire farming folk into poetry of remarkable warmth, wit, and force.

Writing in Scots and English by turns, he ranged from the comic terror of Tam O’ Shanter to the tenderness of A Red, Red Rose and the satire of Holy Willie’s Prayer; his spelling is kept exactly as printed here.

poets.name: Ivan Dmitriev
bio: Ivan Ivanovich Dmitriev (1760–1837), born in the Simbirsk province, was a poet of the sentimental school and a close friend of Karamzin. He is best known for his songs and fables, and later served as Minister of Justice (1810–1814).
