The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Semyon Bobrov
bio: Semyon Sergeyevich Bobrov (c. 1763–1810) was a poet and official. His long poem Khersonida (1804), set in the Crimea, is the source of the three pieces given here; Bowring calls it “an oriental epic poem”. His writing is known for its obscure, ornate style.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Ivan Dolgorukov
bio: Prince Ivan Mikhailovich Dolgorukov (1764–1823) was a courtier, poet and memoirist. Bowring includes his poem “The Legacy” in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Şeyh Galip
bio: Mehmed Esad, known as Şeyh Galip or Galib Dede (1757–1799), was a Mevlevi dervish and sheikh of the Galata convent in Istanbul, and one of the foremost poets of the late Ottoman Romantic school. Sultan Selim III conferred on him the office of sheikh.

His masterpiece is the mystical romance Husn ü Aşk ('Beauty and Love'), from which two passages are given here. E. J. W. Gibb, who gave the first English account of his diwan, praised the strong and glowing verse of his lyric poems.

poets.name: Nikolay Karamzin
poets.credit: Portrait of Nikolay Karamzin by Vasily Tropinin (1818) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Nikolay Mikhailovich Karamzin (1766–1826), born near Simbirsk, was the leading figure of Russian sentimentalism. His Letters of a Russian Traveller (1791–92) and the tale Poor Liza (1792) set a new, polished prose style, and his History of the Russian State (begun 1803, published from 1818) made him a national writer. Bowring called him “the most successful and the most popular” of Russia’s living writers.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Grigory Khovansky
bio: Grigory Khovansky (1767–1796) was a minor Russian poet of the late eighteenth century who died young. Bowring prints one of his songs in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Nikolay Shatrov
bio: Nikolay Ivanovich Shatrov (1767–1841) was a Russian poet who wrote patriotic odes. Bowring prints his ode “To the Army of the Don”, written during the war with Napoleon. Bowring’s volumes give no separate notice of his life, so the dates are those supplied by the archive’s editor.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Ivan Krylov
poets.credit: Portrait of Ivan Krylov by Karl Bryullov (1839) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ivan Andreyevich Krylov (1769–1844) began as a satirical journalist and playwright. He turned to fables in 1809, many adapted from La Fontaine and Aesop, and became Russia’s best-loved fabulist; from 1812 he worked at the Imperial Public Library in St Petersburg. Bowring printed two of his fables in the first part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: William Wordsworth
poets.credit: ‘Wordsworth on Helvellyn’ by Benjamin Robert Haydon (1842) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Wordsworth (1770–1850) was an English Romantic poet who, with Coleridge, launched the movement in Lyrical Ballads (1798).
He made ordinary life and the natural world his subject, and served as Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death.

poets.name: Sir Walter Scott
bio: Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832) was a Scottish poet and novelist whose verse romances — The Lay of the Last Minstrel, Marmion, The Lady of the Lake — made him the best-selling poet in Europe before Byron eclipsed him, and whose Waverley novels effectively invented the historical novel.

Trained as a lawyer in Edinburgh, Scott drew on a lifelong passion for Scottish Border ballads and Highland history; a private financial ruin late in life led him to write at a furious pace to pay off his debts, at the cost of his health.

poets.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
poets.credit: Portrait of Coleridge at age 42 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) was an English poet, critic, and philosopher, co-founder of the Romantic movement.
His visionary poems ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’ and ‘Kubla Khan’ remain touchstones of the imagination he spent his life theorising.

poets.name: Robert Southey
bio: Robert Southey (1774–1843) was an English poet and man of letters, Poet Laureate from 1813 until his death, and one of the “Lake Poets” alongside his friends Wordsworth and Coleridge (whose sister-in-law he married).

He was, in his own day, best known for his grim and often macabre ballads of guilt, folklore and the supernatural, and for prose-poem “Eclogues” that gave a plain, compassionate voice to the rural poor — work that has aged rather better than the long epics on which he staked his reputation.

poets.name: Matthew Arnold
poets.credit: Portrait of Matthew Arnold · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Matthew Arnold (1822–1888) was an English poet and cultural critic, Professor of Poetry at Oxford.
His poems — among them ‘Dover Beach’ and ‘The Scholar-Gipsy’ — register the anxious loss of religious certainty at the heart of the Victorian age.

poets.name: Walter Savage Landor
bio: Walter Savage Landor (1775–1864) was an English writer best known for Imaginary Conversations, a vast series of prose dialogues between historical figures, and for a small body of exquisitely polished short poems and epigrams that later poets — Swinburne, Pound, and others — prized above almost anything else of his era for their classical restraint.

Quarrelsome and litigious by temperament (he was expelled from Oxford and later drove himself into exile in Italy more than once), Landor lived to eighty-nine, still writing crisp, controlled verse almost to the end — including his own epitaph-poem, ‘I strove with none.’

poets.name: Thomas Campbell
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Campbell by Sir Thomas Lawrence · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Campbell (1777–1844) was a Scottish poet, born in Glasgow, the youngest of eleven children. He made his name at twenty-one with The Pleasures of Hope (1799), a didactic poem on hope, liberty and the wrongs of Poland and Africa, and followed it with the Pennsylvania tale Gertrude of Wyoming (1809).

He is best remembered for his patriotic and martial lyrics — ‘Ye Mariners of England’, ‘The Battle of the Baltic’, ‘Hohenlinden’ — and for the ballads ‘Lord Ullin’s Daughter’ and ‘Lochiel’s Warning’. He was also an early promoter of University College London and served as Lord Rector of Glasgow University; he died at Boulogne and is buried in Westminster Abbey.

poets.name: Alexey Merzlyakov
bio: Alexey Fyodorovich Merzlyakov (1778–1830) was a poet and critic and professor of rhetoric at Moscow University. His songs written in the folk manner were widely sung in Russia. Bowring prints his version of Isaiah’s oracle on the fall of Babylon and a pastoral “Duett”.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Thomas Moore
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Moore by Sir Thomas Lawrence (Trinity College, Cambridge; date not given on Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Moore (1779–1852) was Ireland's national poet in the Romantic era, celebrated above all for the Irish Melodies (issued in installments from 1808 to 1834), verses written to fit traditional Irish airs, which carried Irish nationalist feeling and folklore to drawing rooms across Britain and America.

A close friend of Byron (whose memoirs he controversially burned after the poet's death) and a fixture of literary London, Moore was also the author of the wildly popular Oriental verse-romance Lalla Rookh, though it is the Melodies — "The Minstrel Boy," "The Last Rose of Summer," "Believe Me, if All Those Endearing Young Charms" — that have lasted.

poets.name: Alexander Voeikov
bio: Alexander Fyodorovich Voeikov (1779–1839) was a poet, critic and translator, and for a time a professor at the University of Dorpat. Bowring prints his poem “To My Future Bride” in the second part of the Specimens.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Théophile Gautier
poets.credit: Portrait of Théophile Gautier by Nadar, c. 1856 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Théophile Gautier (1811–1872) was a French poet, novelist and critic, born in Tarbes and raised in Paris, where he first trained as a painter before turning to literature. A champion of Romanticism from the 1830s and the principal voice of "art for art's sake", he served as a journalist and theatre critic for most of his working life, and he is much admired by later poets, including the Parnassians and Baudelaire, who dedicated Les Fleurs du mal to him.

Émaux et Camées (Enamels and Cameos), first published in 1852 and enlarged until 1872, gathers his polished, sculptural short poems, in which he treats verse as a craft of enamel, marble and carved gem; the closing poem, "Art", is its manifesto. The original poems are in French. The English shown here is the translation by Agnes Lee, published in 1903 in the Complete Works of Théophile Gautier.

poets.name: Robert Browning
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Browning · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Browning (1812–1889) was an English poet and playwright, master of the dramatic monologue — a poem spoken entirely in an invented character's voice.

This selection gathers his early collections Dramatic Lyrics (1842) and Dramatic Romances (1845); his stage plays and longer closet-dramas (Pauline, Paracelsus, Sordello, Pippa Passes) are not included here.

poets.name: Vasily Zhukovsky
poets.credit: Portrait of Vasily Zhukovsky by Karl Bryullov (1837) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Vasily Andreyevich Zhukovsky (1783–1852) was the founder of Russian Romanticism. His free translations and adaptations of English and German poetry, among them Gray’s “Elegy”, Bürger’s ballads and the ballad “Svetlana” (1813), brought a new emotional range to Russian verse. He later served as tutor to the future Alexander II and was an early mentor and friend of Pushkin.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Leigh Hunt
poets.credit: Portrait of Leigh Hunt by Benjamin Robert Haydon · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Leigh Hunt (1784–1859) was an English poet, essayist and editor, best remembered today as the friend and champion of Keats and Shelley. As editor of The Examiner he was imprisoned from 1813 to 1815 for libelling the Prince Regent, and he received visitors in his cell.
His own poems range from the narrative Story of Rimini (1816) to light verse, sonnets and short lyrics. “Abou Ben Adhem” and “Jenny Kiss’d Me” are the two that most readers know.

poets.name: Denis Davydov
bio: Denis Vasilyevich Davydov (1784–1839) was a cavalry officer, a leader of partisan raids against Napoleon’s army in 1812, and the poet of the “hussar” style of lively, convivial verse. Bowring prints a single short poem under the name “Davidov”; the archive’s editor identifies him with Denis Davydov, but Bowring himself gives no notice of the author.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Konstantin Batyushkov
poets.credit: Portrait of Konstantin Batyushkov by an unknown artist (1810s) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Konstantin Nikolayevich Batyushkov (1787–1855), born in Vologda, served as an officer in the Napoleonic wars and was wounded in 1807 and 1813–14. His smooth, sensuous elegies and epistles, drawing on Italian and French models, were a strong influence on the young Pushkin. From about 1821 he suffered from mental illness and wrote nothing more; he died in Vologda in 1855.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Lord Byron
poets.credit: Portrait by Thomas Phillips (1813) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lord Byron (George Gordon Byron, 1788–1824) was an English Romantic poet and satirist, one of the most celebrated — and scandalous — figures of his age.
He died at Missolonghi while supporting the Greek war of independence, and gave his name to the brooding ‘Byronic hero.’

poets.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poets.credit: Portrait by Alfred Clint · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was an English Romantic poet, radical in politics and idealist in temper.
Author of ‘Ozymandias’ and ‘Ode to the West Wind,’ he drowned off the Italian coast before his thirtieth birthday.

poets.name: Pyotr Vyazemsky
bio: Prince Pyotr Andreyevich Vyazemsky (1792–1878) was a poet, critic and wit, a friend of Pushkin and a prominent member of the Arzamas circle. Bowring, who spells the name “Væsemsky”, prints three of his poems in the second part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: Mikhail Milonov
bio: Mikhail Vasilyevich Milonov (1792–1821) was a Russian poet who wrote satires and elegies and died young. Bowring prints his poem “The Fall of the Leaf” in the second part.

The versions here are by John Bowring, from his Specimens of the Russian Poets (Part the First, 1821; Part the Second, 1823), one of the first English anthologies of Russian verse. They are free, rhymed versions, and should be read as period translations rather than as literal renderings.

poets.name: John Clare
bio: John Clare (1793–1864) was an English labouring-class poet, the son of a Northamptonshire farm labourer, whose closely observed poems of birds, insects and the vanishing open fields of his native Helpston mark him as one of the great nature poets in the language.

His early success gave way to poverty and the destruction of the rural world he wrote from, as the enclosure acts fenced in the commons he had grown up roaming. He spent the last decades of his life in asylums, where he continued to write some of his most haunting poems, including "I Am."

poets.name: Felicia Hemans
poets.credit: Portrait of Felicia Hemans by William Edward West (before 1835) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Felicia Hemans (1793–1835), born Felicia Dorothea Browne in Liverpool and raised largely in Wales, published her first volume of poems at fourteen and became one of the most widely read poets of her day, in Britain and in America.

After her husband left for Italy in 1818 she brought up her five sons alone and supported them by her writing. Her best-known collections include Records of Woman (1828) and Songs of the Affections (1830), and poems such as “Casabianca” and “The Homes of England” were learned by heart by generations of schoolchildren. She died in Dublin at forty-one.

poets.name: John Keats
poets.credit: Portrait by William Hilton (c. 1822) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Keats (1795–1821) was an English Romantic poet whose odes are among the most celebrated in the language.
He trained as a surgeon before devoting himself to poetry, and died of tuberculosis in Rome at just twenty-five.

poets.name: Heinrich Heine
poets.credit: Portrait of Heinrich Heine by Moritz Daniel Oppenheim (1831) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Heinrich Heine (1797–1856) was born in Düsseldorf to a Jewish family and studied law at Bonn, Berlin and Göttingen, taking his degree in 1825 after converting to Protestant Christianity. His Book of Songs (Buch der Lieder, 1827), with its plain, musical lyrics of love and disappointment, made him one of the most widely read German poets, and many of its poems were set to music by Schumann, Schubert and Mendelssohn.

In 1831 Heine moved to Paris, where he lived for the rest of his life, writing travel pieces, criticism and satirical verse, among them Germany: A Winter's Tale and Atta Troll. His work was banned in several German states. From the mid-1840s he suffered from a progressive paralysis and spent his last years confined to what he called his mattress-grave, producing the Romancero (1851) and the late poems. The translations here are by Edgar Alfred Bowring (1908 edition of the complete poems, in the original metres).

poets.name: Alexander Pushkin
poets.credit: Portrait of Alexander Pushkin by Orest Kiprensky (1827) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin (1799–1837) was born in Moscow into an old noble family and educated at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum. His early verse brought him fame, and his liberal poems led the authorities to send him into exile in southern Russia in 1820 and then to his family estate at Mikhailovskoye. He is widely regarded as the founder of modern Russian literature and its literary language.

Besides the verse novel Eugene Onegin, the drama Boris Godunov and the narrative poem The Bronze Horseman, he wrote many short lyrics, ballads and tales in verse. He died in St Petersburg in 1837 of a wound received in a duel. The versions here are by Ivan Panin (1888), who aimed at literal, line-for-line renderings, unrhymed, rather than at the music of the originals.

poets.name: Thomas Hood
poets.credit: Unknown artist, National Portrait Gallery, London · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hood (1799–1845) was an English poet and humorist, famous in his own lifetime chiefly for comic verse and outrageous puns, but remembered today at least as much for a handful of serious social poems — above all ‘The Song of the Shirt’ and ‘The Bridge of Sighs’ — written from genuine anger at the suffering of the poor.

Chronically ill for most of his adult life, he supported a family through unrelenting magazine work, editing and writing comic annuals even as his health failed; he died at forty-five, not long after a government pension was finally arranged for him.

poets.name: Elias Lönnrot
poets.credit: Portrait of Elias Lönnrot, artist unknown, nineteenth century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elias Lönnrot (1802–1884) was a Finnish physician and philologist, born in Sammatti in southern Finland. From 1828 he made a series of collecting journeys through Finland and Russian Karelia, on foot, on horseback, by sledge and by canoe, writing down the rune-songs that country singers still chanted from memory. In 1835 he published the first Kalevala, and in 1849 an enlarged edition of fifty runes; the Finnish Literature Society, which he helped to found, issued both.

Lönnrot is the compiler-author of the Kalevala, not its sole poet. The verses are drawn from oral folk songs, which he selected, ordered and joined into a continuous narrative of the hero Wainamoinen, the smith Ilmarinen and the Sampo, in the unrhymed trochaic metre of the tradition. The poem became a foundation of Finnish national culture. He later served as professor of Finnish at Helsinki and compiled a Finnish dictionary. This archive holds John Martin Crawford's 1888 English translation.

poets.name: Thomas Lovell Beddoes
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Lovell Beddoes by Nathan Cooper Branwhite (1824) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Lovell Beddoes (1803–1849) was an English poet, dramatist and physician, educated at Charterhouse and Oxford. He spent most of his adult life on the Continent, studying medicine in Germany and Switzerland.

His great work, the blank-verse tragedy Death’s Jest-Book, was begun in the 1820s and published only after his death in 1850. It is full of grave-haunted lyrics, such as “Dream-Pedlary” and “Old Adam, the Carrion Crow,” for which he is now chiefly read. He died in Basel in 1849.

poets.name: William Barnes
poets.credit: Photograph of William Barnes, 19th century · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Barnes (1801–1886) was an English poet, philologist and clergyman, born at Rushay in the Vale of Blackmore, Dorset. A largely self-taught scholar, he worked as a schoolmaster in Dorchester and later became rector of Winterborne Came, near Dorchester.

He is best known for his poems in the Dorset dialect, collected in three series of Poems of Rural Life in the Dorset Dialect (1844, 1859, 1862) and gathered in one volume in 1879. Thomas Hardy, who knew him in Dorchester, admired him and wrote of his death in a poem.

poets.name: Lionel Johnson
poets.credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Lionel Johnson (1867–1902) was an English poet and critic associated with the Rhymers' Club and the Decadent movement of the 1890s.
A convert to Catholicism, his spare, disciplined verse turned repeatedly to faith, monastic ideals, and the pull of dissipation he struggled against.

poets.name: Oscar Wilde
poets.credit: Portrait of Oscar Wilde · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900) was an Irish poet, playwright, and wit, one of the most celebrated figures of Victorian literary London before his 1895 trial and imprisonment.
His early verse is lush and Romantic in the Keatsian mode, while The Ballad of Reading Gaol, written after his release from prison, is a stark, plainspoken account of suffering and remorse.

poets.name: Thomas Hardy
poets.credit: Portrait of Thomas Hardy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928) is best known as a novelist, but after finishing Jude the Obscure in 1895 he devoted the rest of his long career chiefly to poetry.
His verse is plain-spoken and often bleak, preoccupied with chance, loss, rural Wessex life, and the death of his first wife Emma, which produced some of his most admired elegies.

poets.name: Namık Kemal
poets.credit: Photograph of Namık Kemal, 1878 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Namık Kemal (1840–1888) was an Ottoman poet, journalist, playwright and political thinker, born in Tekirdağ. A leading figure of the Young Ottomans, the reform-minded circle of the Tanzimat era, he argued for liberty, constitutional government and love of the fatherland in newspapers, plays and verse, and was later known as the "poet of the fatherland" (vatan şairi).

His writing brought him repeated trouble with the authorities: he spent years in exile in Europe in the 1860s, and after his patriotic play Vatan yahut Silistre (1873) he was banished to Magosa (Famagusta) in Cyprus. He later served as an Ottoman provincial governor and died on the island of Chios on 2 December 1888. The eight pieces here are taken from Turkish Wikisource, which lists his death year as 1889; the standard date is 1888.

poets.name: Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem
poets.credit: Photograph of Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem, before 1900, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Recaizade Mahmut Ekrem (1847–1914) was a writer of the Tanzimat period, the Ottoman reform era, and one of the figures who helped turn Turkish literature toward new subjects and a plainer prose. He was born in Istanbul. He is remembered above all for his novel Araba Sevdası (1896) and for his critical writing, and he also wrote plays and a good deal of verse.

Nağme-i Seher ('Song of the Dawn') was a collection of his poems, dated 1288 AH (about 1871). It gathers classical forms (tevhîd and na't, praise poems, chronogram verses, gazels) alongside lighter songs (şarkı). The poems below are given in the Vikikaynak (tr.wikisource.org) Latin-alphabet transcription of the 1871 book, which keeps the book's circumflexed Ottoman spelling.

poets.name: William Ernest Henley
poets.credit: Portrait of William Ernest Henley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Ernest Henley (1849–1903) was an English poet and editor whose leg was amputated in youth after tubercular illness, an experience recorded directly in his sequence In Hospital.
He is best remembered for Invictus, and his robust, muscular verse and criticism made him an influential figure among younger writers of the 1890s.

poets.name: A. E. Housman
poets.credit: Portrait of A. E. Housman · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: A. E. Housman (1859–1936) was an English classical scholar and poet whose reputation rests on two slim volumes, A Shropshire Lad (1896) and Last Poems (1922).
His terse, ballad-like lyrics of doomed youth, soldiering, and rural England were composed in a private grief masked by classical restraint.

poets.name: Andrew Lang
poets.credit: Portrait of Andrew Lang · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Andrew Lang (1844–1912) was a Scottish man of letters, folklorist, and translator, remembered today chiefly for his coloured Fairy Books but also a prolific poet.
His verse favours French forms revived by the 1870s ballade craze, along with translations and tributes to French and English poets he admired.

poets.name: Gerard Manley Hopkins
poets.credit: Photograph of Gerard Manley Hopkins, before 1889, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gerard Manley Hopkins (1844–1889) was an English poet, Roman Catholic convert and Jesuit priest. Born in Stratford, Essex, he studied at Balliol College, Oxford, became a Catholic in 1866 under the influence of John Henry Newman, and entered the Society of Jesus in 1868. He burned his early verses on joining the order and wrote little for several years, until the wreck of the Deutschland in December 1875 drew from him the long ode that opened his mature manner.

His poems, built on what he called sprung rhythm and a dense, coined vocabulary of sound and image, found almost no readers in his lifetime. He worked as a teacher and parish priest, and from 1884 as professor of Greek at University College, Dublin, where he wrote the so-called terrible sonnets and died of typhoid in 1889. His friend Robert Bridges published the first collected Poems in 1918, and Hopkins has since been counted among the major Victorian poets.

poets.name: Robert Bridges
poets.credit: Photograph of Robert Bridges, late 19th century, photographer unknown · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Bridges (1844–1930) was an English poet and physician. Born at Walmer in Kent, he was educated at Eton and Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and trained in medicine at St Bartholomew's Hospital, practising until ill health led him to retire in 1882 and devote himself to poetry. He was a close friend of Gerard Manley Hopkins, whose poems he preserved and, in 1918, brought to the public.

His own verse, notable for its delicate lyrics and metrical experiment, including syllabic measures modelled on Milton's Samson Agonistes, appeared in small private editions such as the Daniel Press Poems of 1884. He became Poet Laureate in 1913, published the long philosophical poem The Testament of Beauty in 1929, and died at Boars Hill, near Oxford, in 1930.

poets.name: Paul Verlaine
poets.credit: Photograph of Paul Verlaine by Otto Wegener, 1893 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Paul Verlaine (1844–1896) was a French poet born in Metz and raised in Paris, where he worked briefly as a clerk at the Hôtel de Ville while publishing his first book, Poèmes saturniens (1866). His Fêtes galantes (1869) and La Bonne Chanson (1870), the latter written for his young fiancée Mathilde Mauté, established him as a master of fluid, musical verse among the Parnassian poets.

In 1871 he met Arthur Rimbaud, and in 1873 he was imprisoned in Belgium after shooting him; Romances sans paroles (1874) was written in these years and Sagesse (1881), a book of Catholic devotion, in the aftermath. He later published Jadis et naguère (1884) and Parallèlement (1889), and was named the leading living poet by the Symbolists, though he spent his last years in poverty and illness in Paris. These versions are from Gertrude Hall's English translation of 1895.

poets.name: Amy Levy
poets.credit: Portrait of Amy Levy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Amy Levy (1861–1889) was an English poet and novelist, among the first Jewish women to study at Cambridge, who took her own life at twenty-seven.
Her poems of London street life, unrequited love, and urban melancholy anticipate the modern lyric's compression and irony.

poets.name: George MacDonald
poets.credit: Portrait of George MacDonald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George MacDonald (1824–1905) was a Scottish minister turned author, celebrated for fantasy novels such as Phantastes and The Princess and the Goblin, and a lifelong writer of devotional and reflective verse.
His poems return often to faith, fatherhood, nature, and the soul's struggle toward trust in a loving God.

poets.name: George Meredith
poets.credit: Portrait of George Meredith · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: George Meredith (1828–1909) was an English novelist and poet whose sonnet sequence Modern Love (1862) gave unusually candid, ironic voice to a marriage's collapse.
His nature poetry, especially The Lark Ascending, prizes close observation and intellectual vigour over conventional sentiment.

poets.name: Charles Baudelaire
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Baudelaire by Étienne Carjat (c. 1862) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Baudelaire (1821–1867) was a French poet, critic and translator of Edgar Allan Poe. Born in Paris, he spent his short life in the city's literary and artistic circles, and is widely regarded as a founder of modern poetry and a forerunner of the Symbolists.

His one major collection of verse, Les Fleurs du Mal (1857), drew a prosecution for offending public morality, and six of its poems were suppressed. Its themes of spleen, beauty, desire, the city and death shaped later poets across Europe. These versions are from Cyril Scott's English translation of 1909.

poets.name: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson
poets.credit: Portrait of Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson by Erwin Raupp, before 1909 (restored by Adam Cuerden; National Library of Norway) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson (1832–1910) was a Norwegian poet, novelist, dramatist and public campaigner, one of the “four great ones” of nineteenth-century Norwegian literature. He wrote the words of the national hymn “Yes, We Love This Land Forever,” and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1903.

The poems here are Arthur Hubbell Palmer’s English versions, made in the original meters and published as Poems and Songs (American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1915); Bjørnson’s originals are in Norwegian. Many began as songs inside his peasant tales and plays, such as Synnøve Solbakken and Arne, others as occasional verse for national causes.

poets.name: William Morris
poets.credit: Portrait of William Morris · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Morris (1834–1896) was an English designer, socialist, and poet, a central figure of the Pre-Raphaelite circle whose vast output includes the narrative cycle The Earthly Paradise and the Icelandic-inspired epic Sigurd the Volsung.
In later years his political convictions produced the direct, rallying verse of Chants for Socialists and The Pilgrims of Hope.

poets.name: Rabindranath Tagore
poets.credit: Rabindranath Tagore, 1909 photograph, published in Les Prix Nobel 1913 (1914) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) was a Bengali poet, songwriter, playwright, novelist and educator, born into a prominent family in Calcutta. He wrote chiefly in Bengali, founded a school at Santiniketan, and in 1913 became the first non-European to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.

The poems here are his own English prose renderings of his Bengali verse: Gitanjali (Song Offerings, 1912), the devotional poems that W. B. Yeats introduced to English readers, and The Gardener (1915), a gathering of love lyrics and poems of youth and life. Tagore translated them himself, and the English is often freer than the Bengali, abridging or paraphrasing as he saw fit.

poets.name: Henry Newbolt
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Newbolt · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Newbolt (1862–1938) was an English poet best known for patriotic and naval verse such as Vitài Lampada and Drake's Drum, written to celebrate duty, empire, and the sea.
His confident public rhetoric made him one of the most widely recited poets of the pre-1914 era.

poets.name: Arthur O'Shaughnessy
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur O'Shaughnessy · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur O'Shaughnessy (1844–1881) was an English poet who worked as a herpetologist at the British Museum while publishing richly musical, melancholy verse.
His Ode, beginning "We are the music makers," is his most famous poem and a manifesto for the visionary power of artists.

poets.name: Algernon Charles Swinburne
poets.credit: Portrait of Algernon Charles Swinburne · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Algernon Charles Swinburne (1837–1909) was an English poet notorious in his own day for the sensuous, metrically dazzling, and often scandalous verse of Poems and Ballads.
An ardent republican, he also wrote fervent political verse cheering Italian unification and liberty, alongside a huge later output of odes, elegies, and sonnets.

poets.name: Francis Thompson
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Thompson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Thompson (1859–1907) was an English poet who spent years destitute and addicted to opium on the streets of London before his talent was discovered and he found refuge among Catholic friends.
His best-known poem, The Hound of Heaven, describes a soul fleeing and finally yielding to divine pursuit.

poets.name: Lewis Carroll
poets.credit: Portrait of Lewis Carroll · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lewis Carroll, the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (1832–1898), was an Oxford mathematician best known for the Alice books, whose fondness for nonsense and wordplay also produced a distinctive body of comic and whimsical verse.
The Hunting of the Snark and the parodies collected in Phantasmagoria remain classics of English nonsense poetry.

poets.name: Rudyard Kipling
poets.credit: Portrait of Rudyard Kipling · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was an English author born in Bombay, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907, whose verse gave voice to soldiers, machines, and the British imperial experience in vigorous, ballad-like rhythms.
Poems such as If—, Gunga Din, and Recessional made him one of the most quoted poets in the English language.

poets.name: Alice Meynell
poets.credit: Portrait of Alice Meynell · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alice Meynell (1847–1922) was an English poet, essayist, and suffragist, admired in her lifetime for the precision and restraint of her devout, closely observed lyrics.
A convert to Catholicism, she wrote often of motherhood, nature, and quiet spiritual attention.

poets.name: Arthur Hugh Clough
poets.credit: Portrait of Arthur Hugh Clough · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Arthur Hugh Clough (1819–1861) was an English poet and close friend of Matthew Arnold, whose verse candidly registers the Victorian crisis of religious faith and doubt.
His long poems Amours de Voyage and The Bothie of Tober-na-Vuolich experiment with conversational, unglamorous realism unusual for their time.

poets.name: Ernest Dowson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ernest Dowson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ernest Dowson (1867–1900) was an English poet of the 1890s Decadent movement, associated with the Rhymers' Club, who died of tuberculosis and drink at thirty-two.
His hallmark is a wistful, musical melancholy, most famous in the refrain "I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion," from his poem Non Sum Qualis Eram.

poets.name: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
poets.credit: Portrait of Alfred, Lord Tennyson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892) was Poet Laureate of Great Britain for over four decades and the most popular and representative poet of the Victorian age.
His work ranges from the intimate grief of In Memoriam A.H.H., written for a dead friend, to the martial narrative verse of Enoch Arden and the ballad-like Maud.

poets.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poets.credit: Portrait of Elizabeth Barrett Browning · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1806–1861) was one of the most celebrated English poets of her day, an invalid for much of her youth who eloped to Italy with fellow poet Robert Browning in 1846.
Her Sonnets from the Portuguese, written to Robert during their courtship, remain her best-loved work, alongside socially engaged narrative poems on slavery, child labour, and women's lives.

poets.name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
poets.credit: Portrait of Dante Gabriel Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dante Gabriel Rossetti (1828–1882) was an English poet and painter, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, who worked in sister arts of image and verse throughout his career.
His sonnet sequence The House of Life traces the arc of love and loss with dense, jewelled imagery, while The Blessed Damozel imagines a dead woman watching for her lover from heaven.

poets.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
poets.credit: Portrait of Robert Louis Stevenson · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Robert Louis Stevenson (1850–1894) was a Scottish novelist and poet, best known for Treasure Island and Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, who also wrote widely loved verse.
A Child's Garden of Verses captures the imaginative world of childhood, while Songs of Travel, mostly written in his final years in Samoa, turns to restlessness, distance, and mortality.

poets.name: Charles Kingsley
poets.credit: Portrait of Charles Kingsley · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charles Kingsley (1819–1875) was an English clergyman, novelist, and poet, remembered as a children's author for The Water-Babies and as a muscular-Christian social reformer.
His poems range from the classical narrative Andromeda, written in unrhymed hexameters, to plain-spoken ballads and songs of the sea and English rural life.

poets.name: Edward Lear
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward Lear · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Lear (1812–1888) was an English artist and writer who, alongside a career as a natural history and landscape painter, invented much of the English nonsense verse tradition.
His limericks, alphabets, and songs such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat and The Jumblies, collected across several Book of Nonsense volumes, delight in invented words and gentle absurdity.

poets.name: Jean Ingelow
poets.credit: Portrait of Jean Ingelow · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Jean Ingelow (1820–1897) was an English poet and novelist, immensely popular in her lifetime, admired for narrative ballads and devotional lyrics of home, sea, and childhood.
Her poem The High Tide on the Coast of Lincolnshire (1571), a ballad of a great flood, remained a schoolroom favourite for generations.

poets.name: Edward FitzGerald
poets.credit: Portrait of Edward FitzGerald · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward FitzGerald (1809–1883) was an English writer whose free translation and adaptation of the medieval Persian quatrains of Omar Khayyam, The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, became one of the most quoted poems in the English language.
Reworked by FitzGerald through several editions, its meditations on wine, transience, and fate gave English verse a strikingly fatalistic, epicurean voice unlike anything else in the period.

poets.name: Coventry Patmore
poets.credit: Portrait of Coventry Patmore · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Coventry Patmore (1823–1896) was an English poet best known for The Angel in the House, a long narrative sequence idealizing married domestic love that became one of the era's most influential, and later most contested, poems.
A convert to Catholicism, his later odes turn toward mystical and religious themes.

poets.name: Adelaide Anne Procter
poets.credit: Portrait of Adelaide Anne Procter · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adelaide Anne Procter (1825–1864) was an English poet and social activist, a devout Catholic and one of the best-selling poets of the Victorian era after Tennyson himself.
Her collection Legends and Lyrics gathers narrative ballads and devotional verse, often concerned with charity, suffering, and quiet endurance.

poets.name: Emily Brontë
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Brontë · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Brontë (1818–1848) is best known as the author of Wuthering Heights, but she also wrote intense, visionary lyric poetry, much of it set in the imagined world of Gondal she created with her sister Anne.

Published pseudonymously as "Ellis Bell" alongside her sisters' verse in 1846, her poems of longing, imprisonment, and the moors were far better received by contemporary critics than the sisters' novels first were.

poets.name: Christina Rossetti
poets.credit: Portrait of Christina Rossetti · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Christina Rossetti (1830–1894) was an English poet of devotional intensity and quiet formal mastery, sister of the painter-poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti.
Best known for ‘Goblin Market’ and the carol ‘In the Bleak Midwinter,’ she also wrote Sing-Song (1872), a book of nursery rhymes for children.

poets.name: Walt Whitman
poets.credit: Portrait of Walt Whitman (George Collins Cox, 1887) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Walt Whitman (1819–1892) was an American poet, essayist, and journalist from Long Island, New York, widely regarded as the father of free verse and one of the most influential poets in American literature.

His single, ever-expanding book ‘Leaves of Grass’, first published in 1855 and revised throughout his life into the 1892 ‘deathbed’ edition used here, celebrated democracy, the body, and the American landscape in a sweeping, unrhymed line.

poets.name: Emily Dickinson
poets.credit: Portrait of Emily Dickinson (daguerreotype, c. 1847) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) was an American poet who lived a famously reclusive life in Amherst, Massachusetts, writing nearly 1,800 poems of which barely a dozen were published in her lifetime.

Her tightly compressed, slant-rhymed verse on death, nature, faith, and the inner mind — much of it untitled and left in small hand-sewn booklets — was published posthumously and is now considered among the most original in American literature.

poets.name: Edgar Allan Poe
poets.credit: Portrait of Edgar Allan Poe (daguerreotype, 1849) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) was an American writer, editor, and literary critic best known for tales of mystery and the macabre, but he considered himself first a poet and a founder of the detective and horror genres.

His musical, tightly-wrought verse — including ‘The Raven’, ‘Annabel Lee’, and ‘The Bells’ — explores loss, beauty, and death, and made him one of the most widely imitated poets in the English language.

poets.name: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
poets.credit: Portrait of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (Julia Margaret Cameron, 1868) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–1882) was an American poet and Harvard professor, and by far the most popular and widely read American poet of the 19th century, both at home and in Europe.

A leading figure among the ‘Fireside Poets’, he wrote narrative epics such as ‘The Song of Hiawatha’ and ‘Paul Revere’s Ride’ alongside shorter lyrics on nature, faith, and everyday life, in verse prized for its clarity and musicality.

poets.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
poets.credit: Portrait of Ralph Waldo Emerson (Josiah Johnson Hawes, 1857) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was an American essayist, lecturer, and poet from Concord, Massachusetts, and the leading voice of the Transcendentalist movement, which prized intuition, nature, and individual conscience over inherited tradition.

Best known for essays such as ‘Self-Reliance’ and ‘Nature’, he also wrote compact, philosophical verse — including ‘Concord Hymn’, ‘The Rhodora’, and ‘Brahma’ — that distilled his ideas into poetic form.

poets.name: William Cullen Bryant
poets.credit: Portrait of William Cullen Bryant — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Cullen Bryant (1794–1878) was an American poet and long-time editor of the New York Evening Post, whose meditative nature poetry helped establish a distinctly American Romantic voice.
Written when he was only seventeen, ‘Thanatopsis’ remains his best-known work, and poems such as ‘To a Waterfowl’ and ‘The Prairies’ celebrate the American landscape with a solemn, elevated calm.

poets.name: James Russell Lowell
poets.credit: Portrait of James Russell Lowell (1855) — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: James Russell Lowell (1819–1891) was an American poet, critic, and diplomat from Cambridge, Massachusetts, who edited the Atlantic Monthly and later served as U.S. minister to Spain and Britain.

A member of the ‘Fireside Poets’, he wrote lyric and narrative verse — most famously ‘The Vision of Sir Launfal’ — alongside satirical and abolitionist poetry that engaged directly with the politics of his day.

poets.name: John Greenleaf Whittier
poets.credit: Portrait of John Greenleaf Whittier — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John Greenleaf Whittier (1807–1892) was an American Quaker poet and dedicated abolitionist from Massachusetts, who used verse throughout his life to campaign against slavery and to record New England legend and rural memory.
His long autobiographical poem ‘Snow-Bound’ (1866), recalling his family snowed in at their farmhouse, became one of the most beloved American poems of the 19th century.

poets.name: Oliver Wendell Holmes
poets.credit: Photograph of Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., c. 1879 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (1809–1894) was a Boston physician, Harvard professor of anatomy and physiology, essayist and poet, one of the Fireside Poets who made New England verse a household possession. His 1830 poem “Old Ironsides” is credited with helping to save the frigate Constitution from being broken up.

His genial comic and occasional verse — “The Deacon’s Masterpiece,” “The Last Leaf,” the dinner poems read for his Harvard classmates — sits beside the more serious “The Chambered Nautilus,” first printed in his Atlantic Monthly series “The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table” (1857–58). The poems here follow his collected Poetical Works as issued in 1893.

poets.name: Sidney Lanier
poets.credit: Portrait of Sidney Lanier — Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sidney Lanier (1842–1881) was an American poet and musician from Georgia who served in the Confederate army, was imprisoned as a prisoner of war, and spent much of his short life battling the tuberculosis that eventually killed him.
A trained flautist, he brought a musician’s sense of rhythm and sound to poems such as ‘The Marshes of Glynn’ and ‘The Song of the Chattahoochee’, which celebrate the landscape of the American South.

poets.name: W. B. Yeats
poets.credit: Portrait of W. B. Yeats by George Charles Beresford (1911) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was an Irish poet and dramatist, born in Dublin, who led the Irish literary revival and co-founded the Abbey Theatre. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923 and served as a senator of the Irish Free State.

His poetry moved from the Celtic Twilight lyrics of The Rose and The Wind Among the Reeds, through the harder manner of Responsibilities and The Wild Swans at Coole, to the visionary poems of Michael Robartes and the Dancer and The Tower. The poems here are drawn from his books published up to 1928.

poets.name: Laurence Binyon
poets.credit: Portrait of Laurence Binyon by William Strang (1901) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Laurence Binyon (1869–1943) was an English poet, playwright and art historian, born in Lancaster and educated at St Paul’s School and Oxford. He worked at the British Museum, where he became Keeper of Prints and Drawings and a leading authority on Asian art.

He is best known for “For the Fallen,” published in The Times in September 1914, whose fourth stanza is read at Remembrance services. He also wrote odes, narrative poems and a verse translation of Dante’s Divine Comedy.

poets.name: Mehmet Emin Yurdakul
bio: Mehmet Emin Yurdakul was born in Beşiktaş, Istanbul, in 1869, the son of a fisherman. He made his name with 'Cenge Giderken' ('Going to War'), published in 1897 during the Greco-Turkish War. He wrote in plain spoken Turkish and the syllabic metre of folk poetry instead of the Persian-derived metres of Ottoman court verse, and became known as 'the Turkish poet'.

He served as an Ottoman provincial governor and an Ottoman deputy, and from 1923 until his death in 1944 sat in the Turkish Grand National Assembly. The poems below come from Türk Sazı ('The Turkish Saz', 1914). The text follows the third edition in modern Turkish letters (Atlas Kitabevi, 1979) as transcribed on tr.wikisource.org.

poets.name: Charlotte Mew
poets.credit: Photograph of Charlotte Mew (c. 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Charlotte Mew (1869–1928) was an English poet, born in Bloomsbury, London. She lived for most of her life with her sister and her mother, in straitened circumstances, and published only two books of poems in her lifetime.

The Farmer’s Bride (1916; enlarged in 1921) won the admiration of Thomas Hardy and other poets and made her reputation. Her poems are dramatic and irregular, with voices ranging from a Devon farmer to a nun and a grieving lover. She died in 1928.

poets.name: Cenap Şahabettin
poets.credit: Photograph of Cenap Şahabettin, c. 1900 (unknown photographer) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Cenap Şahabettin (Cenab Şahabeddin) was born in Manastır in 1870 and died in Istanbul in 1934. He trained as a physician and became one of the leading poets of the Servet-i Fünun ("Wealth of Sciences") circle of the 1890s, the group around Tevfik Fikret that brought French Parnassian and Symbolist manners into late Ottoman poetry. His verse is dense with Persian and Arabic vocabulary. The only book of poems he published, Tâmât (1886), is juvenile work in the old divan manner; the poems that made him the movement's most refined and most mocked stylist, Elhan-ı Şita among them, appeared in the periodicals of the 1890s and were never collected in his lifetime. He also wrote travel prose, essays and aphorisms.

A note on the texts: the poems below are the ones printed in periodicals between 1885 and 1925 (Saadet, Sebat, Mekteb, Servet-i Fünûn, Malûmat, Hazine-i Fünûn, Donanma and others), transcribed on tr.wikisource.org from scans of the original issues. They are in the original Turkish, in the Latin-letter transliteration of the Ottoman text that Wikisource uses, and the old spellings (ñ, â, î, û, the apostrophe for ayn) are kept as transcribed. Titles and printing dates follow the table on the author's Wikisource page; the poem's periodical and date stand in place of a book title. The Tâmât volume itself is not included, and a few short pieces (such as Elhan-ı Şita) are given in a modern transliteration.

poets.name: W. H. Davies
poets.credit: Photograph of W. H. Davies by Alvin Langdon Coburn (1913) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: William Henry Davies (1871–1940) was a Welsh poet and writer, born in Newport, Monmouthshire. He spent years as a tramp in America and Britain, losing a foot while trying to jump a freight train, and wrote of that life in The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp (1908).

His short, simple lyrics about birds, flowers, tramps and the poor made him one of the Georgian poets. “Leisure,” first published in Songs of Joy (1911), is his best-known poem; the other poems here are from Foliage (1913).

poets.name: Hilaire Belloc
poets.credit: Portrait of Hilaire Belloc (c. 1917) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hilaire Belloc (1870–1953) was a French-born English writer and Liberal MP, educated at Balliol College, Oxford, who wrote history, travel books, essays, novels and verse. He was a close friend of G. K. Chesterton, and a Catholic apologist.

His verse, from Verses and Sonnets (1896) and Verses (1910), ranges from serious lyrics of Sussex and of faith to comic and satirical ballads such as the “Dedicatory Ode” and “Lines to a Don.” The Cautionary Tales and Bad Child’s Book of Beasts are his best-known children’s verse.

poets.name: John McCrae
poets.credit: Photograph of John McCrae in uniform (c. 1914) by William Notman and Son · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: John McCrae (1872–1918) was a Canadian physician, soldier and poet, born in Guelph, Ontario. He served as a gunner in the South African War and as a medical officer in the First World War, and taught medicine at McGill University.

He wrote “In Flanders Fields” at Ypres in May 1915 after the death of a friend. It was first published in Punch that December and became one of the best-known poems of the war. He died of pneumonia in France in January 1918, and In Flanders Fields and Other Poems appeared in 1919.

poets.name: G. K. Chesterton
poets.credit: Portrait of G. K. Chesterton by Ernest Herbert Mills (1909) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gilbert Keith Chesterton (1874–1936) was an English writer, born in London, known for his journalism, his Father Brown stories and his Christian apologetics, and also a prolific poet. He wrote on politics, history, and literature with a style full of paradox.

His poems range from the rousing ballad “Lepanto” and the long “Ballad of the White Horse” (1911) to comic verses on wine and inns, such as “The Rolling English Road.” The poems here are drawn from The Wild Knight (1900), Poems (1915), Wine, Water and Song (1915), and The Ballad of St. Barbara (1922).

poets.name: Edward Thomas
poets.credit: Photograph of Edward Thomas (c. 1905) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Edward Thomas (1878–1917) was an English-Welsh writer who made his living as a critic, biographer and country writer before turning to poetry in 1914 at the urging of his friend Robert Frost. He wrote nearly all of his poems in the last two and a half years of his life.

He enlisted in 1915 and was killed at Arras on 9 April 1917. His first collection, Poems, appeared in October 1917 under the pseudonym Edward Eastaway, followed by Last Poems in 1918. Quiet and exact, his poems are among the most admired English poems of the war years, although few of them mention the war directly.

poets.name: D. H. Lawrence
poets.credit: Passport photograph of D. H. Lawrence (1929) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: David Herbert Lawrence (1885–1930) was an English novelist, essayist and poet, born in Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, the son of a coal miner. He wrote Sons and Lovers, The Rainbow and Women in Love, and also much poetry from his early lyrics of Nottinghamshire to the free-verse poems of his years abroad.

The poems here come from Love Poems and Others (1913), Look! We Have Come Through! (1917), New Poems (1918) and Birds, Beasts and Flowers (1923), the last of which contains his best-known animal poems. He died in Vence, France, in 1930.

poets.name: Ahmet Haşim
bio: Ahmet Haşim was born in Baghdad in the mid-1880s (sources differ on the year) and came to Istanbul at about twelve, after his mother's death. At the Galatasaray school he discovered French poetry and the Symbolists. In 1909 he joined the Fecr-i Âtî ('Dawn of the Future') group and published his poems in its magazine, Servet-i Fünûn.

He published two books of verse, Göl Saatleri ('Lake Hours', 1921) and Piyale ('The Wine Cup', 1926), made of short, musical poems about evening, water and light. He died in Istanbul on 4 June 1933. The texts below are the original Turkish, taken from tr.wikisource.org.

poets.name: Rupert Brooke
poets.credit: Photograph of Rupert Brooke by Sherril Schell (1913), from Collected Poems (1918) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Rupert Brooke (1887–1915) was an English poet, born at Rugby and educated at King’s College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow. He was a leading figure among the Georgian poets, and travelled in America and the South Seas in 1913–1914.

He joined the Royal Naval Division in 1914 and wrote the sonnet sequence 1914, which includes “The Soldier.” He died of blood poisoning aboard a French hospital ship off the Greek island of Skyros on 23 April 1915, on his way to Gallipoli, and was buried there.

poets.name: Francis Ledwidge
poets.credit: Portrait of Francis Ledwidge, frontispiece to The Complete Poems (1919) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Francis Ledwidge (1887–1917) was an Irish poet, the son of a farm labourer from Slane, County Meath, who worked as a farmhand, miner and road worker. Lord Dunsany read his early verse, encouraged him and arranged the publication of Songs of the Fields (1915).

He enlisted in the Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers, served at Gallipoli, in Serbia and in France, and wrote poems of the Irish countryside and of the war, including an elegy for Thomas MacDonagh. He was killed at Boezinge, near Ypres, on 31 July 1917.

poets.name: Isaac Rosenberg
poets.credit: Self-portrait of Isaac Rosenberg (before 1918) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Isaac Rosenberg (1890–1918) was an English poet and painter, born in Bristol to Jewish immigrant parents from Lithuania and raised in the East End of London. He studied art at the Slade School, and his first pamphlets of verse were printed at his own expense.

He enlisted in 1915 and wrote his war poems, among them “Break of Day in the Trenches” and “Dead Man’s Dump,” in the trenches, scribbling them on scraps of paper. He was killed on 1 April 1918. His Poems, edited by Gordon Bottomley with a memoir by Laurence Binyon, appeared in 1922.

poets.name: Ivor Gurney
bio: Ivor Gurney (1890–1937) was an English poet and composer, born in Gloucester and a chorister at Gloucester Cathedral, who studied music at the Royal College of Music under Stanford. His work is bound up with the Severn valley and the Gloucestershire countryside.

He served as a private with the 2/5th Gloucesters on the Western Front, was wounded and gassed, and published two books of poems in his lifetime, Severn and Somme (1917) and War’s Embers (1919). He suffered a long mental illness and spent his last fifteen years in an asylum, where he went on writing.

poets.name: Wilfred Owen
poets.credit: Portrait of Wilfred Owen (frontispiece to Poems, 1920) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Wilfred Owen (1893–1918) was an English poet and soldier whose unsparing poems of the Western Front made him the best-known poet of the First World War. Only a handful of his poems were published in his lifetime.

He served with the Manchester Regiment, was treated for shell-shock at Craiglockhart, where he met Siegfried Sassoon, and returned to the front in 1918. He won the Military Cross and was killed on 4 November 1918, a week before the Armistice. His Poems, edited by Sassoon, appeared in 1920.

poets.name: Sabahattin Ali
poets.credit: Sabahattin Ali, c. 1940 (photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Sabahattin Ali (1907–1948) was born in Eğridere (now Ardino), in what is today Bulgaria, and trained as a teacher; he studied German in Potsdam and Berlin in the late 1920s and later taught in Anatolian schools. He is better known today as a novelist and short-story writer, the author of Kuyucaklı Yusuf and Kürk Mantolu Madonna (Madonna in a Fur Coat), but he also wrote verse throughout his life, much of it in the plain, song-like rhythms of Turkish folk poetry.

He was imprisoned in 1932 for a satirical quatrain, and again in the 1940s for his political views; the bitterness and longing of that experience colour poems such as Gurbet Hapishanesi ("The Prison of Exile"). He was killed near the Bulgarian border in April 1948 while trying to leave Turkey. Only seven poems, those transcribed on Turkish Wikisource, are given here; many of his best-loved poems are not included.

poets.name: Orhan Veli Kanık
poets.credit: Portrait photograph of Orhan Veli Kanık (photographer unknown) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Orhan Veli Kanık (1914–1950) was born in Istanbul and grew up partly in Ankara, where he studied at the Gazi High School before reading philosophy at Istanbul University. With his school friends Oktay Rifat and Melih Cevdet he published the volume Garip ("Strange") in 1941, prefaced by a manifesto that attacked rhyme, metre, conventional poetic imagery and the idea that poetry needed an elevated vocabulary. The three poets became known as the Garip movement, and the book is regarded as a turning point in modern Turkish poetry.

His own poems are built from the speech of the street, the ferry, the café and the neighbourhood: short lines, everyday objects, humour and an unforced tenderness, with Istanbul, the sea and ordinary people as constant subjects. He followed Garip with further collections, among them Vazgeçemediğim (1945), Destan Gibi (1946), Yenisi (1947) and Karşı (1949), and also worked as a translator and essayist. He died in Istanbul in November 1950, aged thirty-six, after an accident; his plain-speech revolution outlived him and shaped almost every Turkish poet who came after.

poets.name: Rüştü Onur
bio: Rüştü Onur was born in 1920 in Devrek, in the Zonguldak region of Turkey's Black Sea coast. He died of tuberculosis in 1942, aged 22. His friend Muzaffer Tayyip Uslu, another young poet from Zonguldak who also died young of the disease, is remembered beside him: anthologies have long presented the two together as the 'poets of Zonguldak'.

His poems were gathered after his death; a posthumous collection was published by Yeditepe Yayınları in 1956. This is a first instalment of four poems, not his complete poems. The texts are the original Turkish, taken from tr.wikisource.org.

works.title: The Aeneid
works.author: Virgil
works.note: Project Gutenberg #228 carries no title page; Dryden's Virgil was published by Jacob Tonson in 1697, and Dryden died in 1700.
works.blurb: Virgil's Latin epic of Aeneas, the Trojan refugee who carries his gods to Italy and founds the line of Rome, in twelve books, rendered into English heroic couplets by John Dryden.

works.title: Andreas
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation. Once widely attributed to Cynewulf on stylistic grounds; modern scholarship no longer accepts the attribution.
works.blurb: The apostle Andrew's perilous sea voyage to rescue Matthew from the cannibalistic Mermedonians, told in a style deliberately recalling Beowulf's heroic diction.

works.title: The Barons' Wars
works.subtitle: In the Reign of Edward the Second (Books II–VI)
works.author: Michael Drayton
works.blurb: Drayton's verse chronicle of the civil wars under Edward II, in ottava rima — this edition preserves Books II through VI.

works.title: Beowulf
works.author: Beowulf Poet
works.note: Anonymous Old English original; this is Francis Barton Gummere's 1910 alliterative verse translation, prepared for the Harvard Classics and in the public domain.
works.blurb: The Geatish hero Beowulf crosses the sea to rid the Danish hall of Heorot of the monster Grendel, then Grendel's vengeful mother, and in old age faces a dragon guarding a cursed hoard — the oldest surviving epic in English.

sections.title: Prelude of the Founder of the Danish House

works.title: The Canterbury Tales
works.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
works.note: Original Middle English text (modernized spelling, D. Laing Purves edition, 1870s). Unfinished at Chaucer's death; the Cook's Tale breaks off and the Parson's Tale closes the collection in prose.
works.blurb: A fellowship of pilgrims riding from Southwark to Canterbury pass the road in stories — chivalric romance, low comedy, sermon, and fable — in the original Middle English, the foundation of English narrative poetry.

works.title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage
works.author: Lord Byron
works.note: Text of Project Gutenberg #5131, which prints no edition date; the four cantos appeared between 1812 and 1818. Byron's prose preface, the prose dedication of Canto IV and the end-notes are omitted.
works.blurb: Byron's Spenserian travelogue in four cantos follows a world-weary young pilgrim through Portugal, Spain, Greece, Belgium, the Rhine and Italy, turning from personal gloom to meditations on liberty, ruin and the sublime.

works.title: Christ I
works.subtitle: The Advent Lyrics
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation. Unsigned; grouped with Christ II and Christ III in the Exeter Book as a single sequence on the life of Christ, though the three are almost certainly by different, mostly anonymous poets.
works.blurb: A sequence of lyric meditations, based on the liturgical O Antiphons of Advent, anticipating the coming of Christ.

works.title: Christ II
works.subtitle: The Ascension
works.author: Cynewulf
works.note: Prose translation. One of Cynewulf's four signed poems.
works.blurb: Cynewulf's account of Christ's Ascension into heaven, drawing on a homily of Gregory the Great, and of the gifts of grace bestowed on humankind.

works.title: Christ III
works.subtitle: Judgment Day
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation. Unsigned.
works.blurb: A vision of the Last Judgment: Christ's sudden return, the terror of sinners and the joy of the blessed, closing the Exeter Book's Christ sequence.

works.title: Christ and Satan
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: The last poem of the Junius Manuscript: the lament of the fallen angels in hell, Christ's Harrowing of Hell and Ascension, and finally Satan's temptation of Christ in the wilderness.

works.title: Chronicle of the Cid
works.author: Anonymous (Poem of the Cid)
works.note: Prose translation and compilation from medieval Spanish chronicle and ballad sources; not a verse rendering of the Cantar de Mio Cid itself.
works.blurb: Robert Southey’s English compilation of the medieval Spanish chronicles and ballads recounting the life and legend of Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, El Cid.

works.title: Comus
works.subtitle: A Mask Presented at Ludlow Castle
works.author: John Milton
works.blurb: A masque of chastity and temptation, performed at Ludlow Castle in 1634 — a Lady lost in the wood and the enchanter Comus.

works.title: Confessio Amantis
works.subtitle: Tales of the Seven Deadly Sins
works.author: John Gower
works.note: Original Middle English text, edited by G. C. Macaulay (The Works of John Gower, Oxford, 1899–1902).
works.blurb: A lover confesses to Venus's priest Genius, who works through the Seven Deadly Sins with a great gathering of exemplary tales — classical, biblical, and romance — in eight books of octosyllabic couplets.

works.title: Daniel
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: A verse paraphrase of the Book of Daniel: Nebuchadnezzar's pride and madness, the three youths in the fiery furnace, and Belshazzar's feast and the writing on the wall.

works.title: The Divine Comedy
works.subtitle: La Divina Commedia
works.author: Dante Alighieri
works.blurb: Dante's vision of the afterlife in a hundred cantos, from the dark wood through Inferno and Purgatorio to the Paradiso, in Longfellow's blank-verse tercets.

works.title: Don Juan
works.author: Lord Byron
works.note: Text of Project Gutenberg #21700, which follows an 1857 edition; the cantos appeared between 1819 and 1824, and Canto XVII was left a fragment at Byron's death.
works.blurb: Byron's unfinished comic epic in ottava rima follows a young Spaniard through seductions, shipwreck, war and the courts of Europe, mocking cant, politics and poetry itself along the way.

works.title: Elene
works.author: Cynewulf
works.note: One of Cynewulf's four signed poems; his runic signature appears near the close.
works.blurb: Cynewulf's retelling of the legend of St. Helena, mother of the Emperor Constantine, and her journey to Jerusalem in search of the True Cross, opening with Constantine's vision of the Cross before his battle at the Milvian Bridge.

works.title: Endymion
works.subtitle: A Poetic Romance
works.author: John Keats
works.note: Text of the 1818 first edition, from Project Gutenberg #24280. Printer's errata are left as printed; the Preface and dedication are omitted.
works.blurb: Keats's four-book retelling of the myth of the shepherd prince Endymion, loved by the moon goddess and wandering the earth, sea and underworld in search of her.

works.title: An Essay on Man
works.subtitle: In Four Epistles to Henry St John, Lord Bolingbroke
works.author: Alexander Pope
works.blurb: Pope’s attempt, in polished couplets, to ‘vindicate the ways of God to Man’ — four epistles on man’s place in the universe, himself, society, and happiness.

works.title: Exodus
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation.
works.blurb: A dense, martial retelling of the Israelites' flight from Egypt and crossing of the Red Sea, cast largely in the diction of Old English heroic poetry.

works.title: The Faerie Queene
works.subtitle: Books I–VI, with the Mutabilitie Cantos
works.author: Edmund Spenser
works.blurb: Spenser's vast allegorical epic of knights, virtues, and the Faerie court — six completed Books (Holinesse, Temperaunce, Chastitie, Friendship, Iustice, Courtesie) plus the fragmentary Mutabilitie Cantos, in the original 1590s spelling.

works.title: The Fates of the Apostles
works.author: Cynewulf
works.note: Prose translation. One of Cynewulf's four signed poems; his runic signature closes it.
works.blurb: A brief martyrology recounting, in turn, the missionary travels and deaths of Christ's twelve apostles, closing the Vercelli Book poem with Cynewulf's runic signature.

works.title: Genesis
works.subtitle: Genesis A and Genesis B
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation. Once attributed to Caedmon; the manuscript's Genesis is now known to be composite, a longer Genesis A into which a distinct poem, Genesis B (itself apparently translated from an Old Saxon original), was inserted.
works.blurb: A verse paraphrase of Genesis running from the Creation and the fall of the rebel angels through Abraham and the near-sacrifice of Isaac, opening the Junius Manuscript.

works.title: Gondibert
works.subtitle: An Heroick Poem
works.author: Sir William Davenant
works.blurb: Davenant’s unfinished heroic poem in decasyllabic quatrains — three books and twenty cantos of love, war and statecraft among the Lombards.

works.title: Guthlac
works.subtitle: Guthlac A and Guthlac B
works.author: Anonymous (Old English)
works.note: Prose translation of both Guthlac A and Guthlac B, presented here as Kennedy translated them, as one continuous work. Guthlac B breaks off mid-sentence at the end of a damaged manuscript page.
works.blurb: The life of St. Guthlac of Crowland, a former warrior turned hermit who does battle with demons in the Lincolnshire fens (Guthlac A), and an account, closely based on Felix's Latin Life, of his final illness and death (Guthlac B).

works.title: The Hind and the Panther
works.subtitle: A Poem, in Three Parts
works.author: John Dryden

poems.title: The Seafarer
poems.excerpt:
I can utter a true song about myself, tell of my travels, how in toilsome days I often suffered a time of hardship, how I have borne bitter sorrow in my breast, made trial of many sorrowful abodes on ships; dread was the rolling of the waves. There the hard night-watch at the boat's prow was often my task, when it tosses by the cliffs. Afflicted with cold, my feet were fettered by frost, by chill bonds. There my sorrows, hot round my heart, were sighed forth; hunger within rent the mind of the sea-weary man. The man who fares most prosperously on land knows not how I, careworn, have spent a winter as an exile on the ice-cold sea, cut off from kinsmen, hung round with icicles. The hail flew in showers. I heard naught there save the sea booming, the ice-cold billow, at times the song of the swan. I took my gladness in the cry of the gannet and the sound of the curlew instead of the laughter of men, in the screaming gull instead of the drink of mead. There storms beat upon the rocky cliffs; there the tern with icy feathers answered them; full often the dewy-winged eagle screamed around. No protector could comfort the heart in its need. And yet he who has the bliss of life, who, proud and flushed with wine, suffers few hardships in the city, little believes how I often in weariness had to dwell on the ocean path. The shadow of night grew dark, snow came from the north, frost bound the earth; hail fell on the ground, coldest of grain. And yet the thoughts of my heart are now stirred that I myself should make trial of the high streams, of the tossing of the salt waves; the desire of the heart always exhorts to venture forth that I may visit the land of strange people far hence. And yet there is no man on earth so proud, nor so generous of his gifts, nor so bold in youth, nor so daring in his deeds, nor with a lord so gracious unto him, that he has not always anxiety about his seafaring, as to what the Lord will bestow on him. His thoughts are not of the harp, nor of receiving rings, nor of delight in a woman, nor of joy in the world, nor of aught else save the rolling of the waves; but he who sets out on the waters ever feels longing. The groves put forth blossoms; cities grow beautiful; the fields are fair; the world revives; all these urge the heart of the eager-minded man to a journey, him who thus purposes to fare far on the ways of the flood. Likewise the cuckoo exhorts with sad voice; the harbinger of summer sings, bodes bitter sorrow to the heart. The man knows not, the prosperous being, what some of those endure who most widely pace the paths of exile. And yet my heart is now restless in my breast, my mind is with the sea-flood over the whale's domain; it fares widely over the face of the earth, comes again to me eager and unsatisfied; the lone-flier screams, resistlessly urges the heart to the whale-way over the stretch of seas.

Wherefore the joys of the Lord are more inspiring for me than this dead fleeting life on earth. I have no faith that earthly riches will abide for ever. Each one of three things is ever uncertain ere its time comes; illness or age or hostility will take life away from a man doomed and dying. Wherefore the praise of living men who shall speak after he is gone, the best of fame after death for every man, is that he should strive ere he must depart, work on earth with bold deeds against the malice of fiends, against the devil, so that the children of men may later exalt him and his praise live afterwards among the angels for ever and ever, the joy of life eternal, delight amid angels. …

poems.excerpt: Father and mother gave me up dead in these days, nor was life or stir yet within me. The beautiful kinswoman afterwards fed me, till I grew up, could set out more widely on journeys; she had the fewer of her own dear sons and daughters by what she did thus.
